Usage

Caches.fanout(name)


A NullCache while it can’t be opened or is disabled, exactly as for a plain cache. That includes a directory whose layout doesn’t match the registration (LayoutMismatchError: a plain cache’s directory, or settings too small for the folder’s shard count): reported through on_open_error, remembered, and retried after retry_open_after. A folder with another shard count than the registered one is not an error: it opens with its own count, and the registry logs a WARNING (see the class docs). title: Cache.close()
text:
Close this handle and return its connections.


Usage
Source


Cache.close(*, checkpoint=True)


When the last handle on a directory in the process closes, every connection to it closes, whichever threads used them, and the folders that large values use are swept (D-042): a temp file no writer has touched for an hour, left by a process killed mid-write, is removed, and a folder left empty goes (those not touched in the last 30 seconds), for at most 100 ms in all, unless this thread is inside a transaction. A handle dropped without close() does the same. Using the cache again afterwards reopens it.
It never raises. Behind a fork that stays stuck it returns after about 2 seconds at most, whatever timeout is, and those connections close when the fork ends.


Parameters


checkpoint: bool = True

If this is the process’s last handle and the write-ahead log is over half of wal_size_limit, checkpoint it first, waiting at most 1 second. A small log costs nothing extra.





Examples
with Cache('/var/cache/my-app') as cache:   # closed at the end of the block
    cache.set('k', 'v')
cache.close(checkpoint=False)                # skip the checkpoint, for a quick exit

title: Caches.register()
text:
Register a cache. Nothing opens until its first lookup.


Usage
Source


Caches.register(name, *, directory=None, **settings)


Parameters


name: N

The cache’s name. Without directory, it’s also the directory’s name under base_dir, so it must be a plain name: no path separators, not . or ...

directory: str | os.PathLike[str] | None = None

Put this cache somewhere else.

**settings: Any

Cache settings for this cache, over the registry’s defaults. A callable on_decode_error is called as (name, key, exc), as at the registry level. Adding shards= registers a FanoutCache instead, which takes the same settings; read it with fanout(name). shards=n is the count for a new folder: an existing one keeps the count it was created with, and the registry warns when that isn’t n. Passing the key at all is what picks the kind, so shards=None is NOT “not sharded”: it is a FanoutCache with the stored shard count, or 8 for a new root. Leave shards out for a plain cache (a config file that writes shards: null for “none” would register a FanoutCache).





Raises


 ValueError

The name is taken or isn’t a plain directory name, or another registered cache already uses that directory (two names would share one store, and the last one opened would quietly set its size_limit).

 TypeError

An unknown Cache (or FanoutCache) setting.





Examples

caches.register('rate_limits', shards=8)            # a FanoutCache; read with fanout()

title: FanoutCache
text:
A disk cache split over several SQLite databases (shards), so reads and writes on different keys


Usage
Source


FanoutCache(
    directory,
    timeout=None,
    *,
    shards=None,
    size_limit=None,
    cull_limit=None,
    serializer="msgpack",
    pickle=False,
    types=None,
    clock=None,
    max_connections=None,
    sqlite_cache_size=None,
    wal_size_limit=None,
    wal_checkpoint="manual",
    on_decode_error=None,
    durable=False
)


don’t queue on one file’s locks.
Each key lives in exactly one shard, chosen by a hash that is part of the on-disk format: every process, and every release, sends a key to the same shard. The root records its shard count, so every handle agrees on it. Single-key calls behave exactly as on Cache, on the key’s shard. len() and volume() add up every shard under one timeout.
clear(), expire(), cull() and checkpoint() run on every shard in turn, under one timeout for the whole call. If a shard fails, the others are still done, and then the first failure raises, as its own type (so except Timeout still works), with two extra attributes and a note naming them:

failed_shards: a tuple of the indexes of the shards that failed, in order.
removed (not on checkpoint()): how many entries the call removed in all, from every shard, including what a failed shard removed before it failed.



Parameters


directory: str | os.PathLike[str]

The root directory. It holds the manifest (diskcache-oxide-fanout) and one directory per shard, 000 to NNN. It must not be a plain Cache’s directory.

timeout: float | None = None

As for Cache (default 60). Opening, len(), volume(), clear(), expire(), cull(), checkpoint() and close() share one timeout across every shard, not one each.

shards: int | None = None

How many shards, 1 to 256. None (the default) uses the count the root records, or 8 for a new root. A count that differs from the recorded one raises LayoutMismatchError (a ValueError): changing it needs a new directory. Each shard takes about 4 file descriptors to open, and 2 more per connection it opens in use, so 256 shards need over 1,024: more than Linux’s default ulimit -n. Too few raises OSError (EMFILE) with the numbers.

size_limit: int | None = None

The disk budget in bytes for the whole cache, split evenly (floored) across the shards, each of which culls on its own. Each shard needs at least 1 MiB, so the total must be at least shards MiB. With none given, a new root gets 1 GiB in all.

cull_limit: int | None = None

As for Cache, per shard.

serializer: str = "msgpack"

As for Cache.

pickle: bool = False

As for Cache.

clock: Callable[[], float] | None = None

As for Cache.

max_connections: int | None = None

The most SQLite connections this process opens for the whole cache, split across the shards (the first max_connections % shards get one more). At least shards. The default is two per shard, and never fewer than 8 in all.

sqlite_cache_size: int | None = None

As for Cache, per connection.

wal_size_limit: int | None = None

As for Cache, per shard (each shard has its own write-ahead log).

wal_checkpoint: Literal["manual", "auto"] = "manual"

As for Cache.

on_decode_error: Literal["raise", "miss"] | Callable[[str, Exception], object] | None = None

As for Cache.

durable: bool = False

As for Cache: single-key calls on a shard that fails give their miss values. One report covers every shard, named by the root directory.





Raises


 ValueError

A setting is out of range, or max_connections is below shards.

 LayoutMismatchError

shards differs from the root’s, or the directory belongs to a plain Cache (or a shard of it does). Also a ValueError, and a FormatMismatchError.

 TypeError

An argument has the wrong type, including a bool for timeout or shards.

 FormatMismatchError

The root’s manifest, or a shard’s database, is in a format this version can’t read.

 OSError

The filesystem doesn’t support hard links, which creating the manifest needs, or the process can’t open enough files for every shard (ulimit -n).

 Timeout

A shard stayed locked, or a fork stayed pending, for longer than timeout.





Examples
from diskcache_oxide import FanoutCache

cache = FanoutCache('/var/cache/my-app-counters', shards=8)   # shards is keyword-only
cache.incr('ip:203.0.113.7')          # as on Cache, on the key's shard
cache.shard_of('ip:203.0.113.7')      # 0 to 7, the same in every process and release
with cache.transact(key='totals') as tx:   # one shard's write lock, not all of them
    tx.set('totals', tx.get('totals', 0) + 1)

title: Single-use keys
text: At 2 a.m. a tired user double-clicks a password reset link, and two requests arrive on two workers a few milliseconds apart. Both find the token. Both accept it. Some things must happen exactly once however many times they’re asked for: a reset link is good for one click, a verification code for one entry, a payment request for one charge even when the client retries. Two cache calls are atomic across every worker on the machine, pop() and add(), and between them they cover all of these.

title: Single-use keys
section: Short codes need an attempt limit
text:
Short codes need an attempt limit
A six-digit verification code is guessable, so pair it with a counter, created with an expiry the way the rate limiting recipe does, and burn the code after a few wrong guesses:
def check_code(user_id: int, entered: str) -> bool:
    attempts_key = f'verify-attempts:{user_id}'
    tokens.add(attempts_key, 0, expire=10 * 60)
    if tokens.incr(attempts_key) > 5:
        tokens.delete(f'verify-code:{user_id}')   # too many tries: the code is dead
        return False
    if tokens.get(f'verify-code:{user_id}') != entered:
        return False
    tokens.delete(f'verify-code:{user_id}')       # right, and good for one entry only
    return True

title: Using the cache from asyncio
text: An async framework makes one promise to every request it’s serving: nothing blocks the loop. A synchronous cache call looks like a small risk to that promise, and whether it is depends entirely on which call. diskcache-oxide’s API is synchronous. An AsyncCache is on the roadmap, but the sync cache already works well in an asyncio app, provided you know which calls can block the event loop and for how long. Here are the three rules.

title: Using the cache from asyncio
text:
Fire and forget
When the response shouldn’t wait for the write at all, schedule it as a task. Keep a reference to the task until it finishes, or the loop may drop it half done:
background: set[asyncio.Task] = set()

def cache_later(key: str, value: object, expire: float) -> None:
    task = asyncio.create_task(asyncio.to_thread(cache.set, key, value, expire=expire))
    background.add(task)
    task.add_done_callback(background.discard)

title: Sharing a cache across web workers
text: Deployment is where a cache meets the real world: several worker processes that don’t know each other’s names, a server that forks and recycles them while they’re busy, a cron job that opens the same directory on the side. diskcache-oxide is built for exactly this, so there isn’t much to it. This page covers the few choices that matter and leaves out the ones that don’t.

title: Caching responses from other services
text:
Your dashboard endpoint takes 1.2 seconds, and 1.1 of them are spent waiting for a partner API to return the same JSON it returned to the previous request. An app that calls other services (a payments API, a headless CMS, your own microservices) spends most of its latency waiting on them, and most of those answers don’t change between calls. Caching them in a directory every worker shares means one request to the upstream per machine instead of one per worker, and a last known good answer to serve when the upstream is slow, or down, or has started returning the wrong thing with a 500.

A cached fetch
The entry holds the response body, its ETag and a freshness deadline taken from the upstream’s Cache-Control: max-age, with a default when there isn’t one. A fresh entry is returned without a request. A stale one is revalidated with If-None-Match, so an unchanged resource costs a 304 with no body. And if the request fails while there’s a stale entry, the stale entry is the answer.

import json
import re
import tempfile

import httpx

from diskcache_oxide import Cache

now = [1_000_000.0]                                   # a fake clock; in a real app use time.time()
cache = Cache(tempfile.mkdtemp(), clock=lambda: now[0])

def max_age(response: httpx.Response) -> float | None:
    m = re.search(r'max-age=(\d+)', response.headers.get('cache-control', ''))
    return float(m.group(1)) if m else None

def fetch_json(client: httpx.Client, url: str, *, default_ttl: float = 300, keep: float = 24 * 3600) -> object:
    key = f'http:GET:{url}'
    entry = cache.get(key)
    if entry is not None and now[0] < entry['fresh_until']:
        return json.loads(entry['body'])              # fresh: no request at all

    headers = {'If-None-Match': entry['etag']} if entry and entry['etag'] else {}
    try:
        response = client.get(url, headers=headers)
        if response.status_code != 304:
            response.raise_for_status()
    except httpx.HTTPError:
        if entry is not None:
            return json.loads(entry['body'])          # upstream trouble: the last good answer
        raise

    if response.status_code == 304:                   # unchanged: keep the body, extend its freshness
        entry['fresh_until'] = now[0] + (max_age(response) or default_ttl)
    else:
        entry = {
            'body': response.content,
            'etag': response.headers.get('etag'),
            'fresh_until': now[0] + (max_age(response) or default_ttl),
        }
    cache.set(key, entry, expire=keep)
    return json.loads(entry['body'])

Here it runs against a mock upstream that counts its requests:

seen: list[str | None] = []

def upstream(request: httpx.Request) -> httpx.Response:
    seen.append(request.headers.get('If-None-Match'))
    headers = {'ETag': '"v1"', 'Cache-Control': 'max-age=60'}
    if request.headers.get('If-None-Match') == '"v1"':
        return httpx.Response(304, headers=headers)
    return httpx.Response(200, json={'episodes': [512, 513]}, headers=headers)

client = httpx.Client(transport=httpx.MockTransport(upstream))
url = 'https://api.example.com/episodes'

fetch_json(client, url)
fetch_json(client, url)                               # fresh: served from the cache
now[0] += 61
fetch_json(client, url)                               # stale: one conditional request, answered 304
print(f'{len(seen)} upstream requests; If-None-Match headers sent: {seen}')

2 upstream requests; If-None-Match headers sent: [None, '"v1"']


Why it’s shaped this way:

Freshness lives in the value, not in expire. The entry’s expire (keep) is how long a stale copy is worth holding on to for revalidation and outages. If freshness were the expiry, a stale entry would vanish just when it’s useful.
304 costs one small write. The body is kept and only fresh_until changes. A set() is needed because the deadline is inside the value; touch() only moves the entry’s expiry.
The key names the request. Method and URL here. If the response depends on who’s asking (an Authorization header, a tenant), put that identity in the key too, or one user’s data will be served to another.



Variations

Serving the bytes straight through. When your endpoint relays the upstream’s body, store response.content and the content-type, and return them as they are, without parsing. Bodies of 64 KiB or more are stored in their own file, so a large payload costs no more than a small one.
Negative caching. A 404 that costs a round trip every time is worth caching for a short while: store {'status': 404, 'fresh_until': ...} and return your own not-found from it. Don’t cache 5xx as answers; the stale-on-error path above already covers an upstream outage.
Headers not to keep. Drop Set-Cookie and anything else tied to the one connection before storing a response’s headers.
Only one worker should refetch. When many requests find the same stale entry at once, they all revalidate. 304s are cheap, so that’s usually fine. If the upstream charges per call, wrap the refetch in a claim as the stale-while-revalidate recipe does.

title: Server-side sessions
text:
Every request arrives with a cookie and a question: who is this? A session is the one piece of per-user state almost every web app keeps server side to answer it: who’s logged in, since when, with which roles. Keeping it in a cache directory means every worker sees the same session the instant it’s written, a login on one worker is a login on all of them, and there’s no database row per request and no Redis to run. The cookie holds only a random id.

Start, load, end

import secrets
import tempfile

from diskcache_oxide import Cache

now = [1_000_000.0]                                   # a fake clock; in a real app use time.time()
sessions = Cache(tempfile.mkdtemp(), clock=lambda: now[0])

IDLE = 30 * 60          # a session ends after 30 minutes without a request
ABSOLUTE = 12 * 3600    # and 12 hours after login, however active

def start_session(user_id: int, roles: list[str]) -> str:
    sid = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
    sessions.set(f'session:{sid}', {'user_id': user_id, 'roles': roles, 'started': now[0]}, expire=IDLE)
    sessions.set(f'user-sessions:{user_id}:{sid}', True, expire=ABSOLUTE)
    return sid

def load_session(sid: str) -> dict | None:
    data, expires_at = sessions.get(f'session:{sid}', expire_time=True)
    if data is None or now[0] - data['started'] > ABSOLUTE:
        return None
    if expires_at - now[0] < IDLE / 2:                # slide the idle timeout, but not on every request
        sessions.touch(f'session:{sid}', expire=IDLE)
    return data

def end_session(sid: str) -> None:
    data = sessions.pop(f'session:{sid}')
    if data is not None:
        sessions.delete(f'user-sessions:{data["user_id"]}:{sid}')

sid = start_session(42, ['member'])
now[0] += 20 * 60
print('after 20 min:', load_session(sid) is not None)   # active, and the timeout slides
now[0] += 20 * 60
print('after 40 min:', load_session(sid) is not None)   # still active: the last request was 20 min ago
now[0] += 31 * 60
print('after 71 min:', load_session(sid) is not None)   # idle too long

after 20 min: True
after 40 min: True
after 71 min: False



touch() slides the idle timeout without rewriting the session. It’s a small write, so it’s done only when less than half the idle time is left, which get(expire_time=True) tells you in the same read as the data. A busy user costs one write every 15 minutes instead of one per request.
The absolute lifetime is inside the value. expire can only say when the session dies if it’s left alone; the login time says when it dies regardless.
The id is the secret. secrets.token_urlsafe(32) in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie, and nothing else in the cookie. The session dict holds ids and roles, not the whole user object, which belongs in the database.



Log out everywhere
A password change or a stolen laptop should end every session a user has. The second key written at login, user-sessions:{user_id}:{sid}, is an index for exactly this: a prefix scan finds them all.

other = start_session(42, ['member'])
sid = start_session(42, ['member'])

def end_all_sessions(user_id: int) -> int:
    ended = 0
    for key in sessions.iterkeys(prefix=f'user-sessions:{user_id}:'):
        sid = key.rsplit(':', 1)[1]
        ended += sessions.delete(f'session:{sid}')
        sessions.delete(key)
    return ended

print(end_all_sessions(42), 'sessions ended;', 'still valid:', load_session(other) is not None)

2 sessions ended; still valid: False


Index entries for sessions that idled out stay until their own ABSOLUTE expiry, which is why they have one. To show a user their active sessions, read each session: key the index names and skip the ones that are gone.


Sessions are not cache entries
A lost session is a forced logout, so sessions get a cache of their own, configured unlike the one for page fragments:

A size_limit it never reaches. Eviction removes the least recently stored entries, and a long-lived session is exactly that. Sessions are small (a few hundred bytes each), so even 1 GiB, the default, holds millions. Watch volume() if you store more per session.
Never a NullCache. A NullCache stores nothing, so nobody could log in. If the app’s other caches can be switched off through Caches, register the session cache by name and leave it enabled.
Not durable=True. A dropped write there means a login that silently didn’t happen. Let set() raise and show the user an error.
Run expire() from a scheduled job, claimed by one worker, so ended sessions free their space. Expired sessions are already invisible to get(); this is housekeeping.
One machine. Every worker on the host shares the sessions. Behind a load balancer, use sticky sessions or wait for the network server.

title: Rate limiting
text:
Someone has pointed a script at your search endpoint. It’s a polite script: it stays under your limit of 100 requests a minute. Per worker. With eight workers and an in-memory counter in each, the limit you meant is 100 and the limit you have is 800. To limit each client for real, every worker process has to see the same count, and Redis is the usual fix. A diskcache-oxide counter is shared by every worker on the machine, and incr() is atomic across processes, so concurrent requests never lose a count.

A fixed-window limiter
Each client gets a counter for the current window, with the window’s number in the key. When the window ends, requests move on to a new key and the old one simply expires.

import tempfile

from diskcache_oxide import Cache

now = [1_000_000.0]  # a fake clock, so this example can move time forward
cache = Cache(tempfile.mkdtemp(), clock=lambda: now[0])

def allow_request(client: str, limit: int = 5, window: int = 60) -> bool:
    current = int(now[0] // window)          # in a real app: int(time.time() // window)
    key = f'rate:{client}:{current}'
    cache.add(key, 0, expire=window * 2)     # start the window's counter, once
    return cache.incr(key) <= limit

print([allow_request('203.0.113.9') for _ in range(7)])

now[0] += 60  # the next window
print(allow_request('203.0.113.9'))

[True, True, True, True, True, False, False]
True


Why it’s built this way:

add() then incr(). add() creates the counter with an expiry the first time and does nothing after that. incr() keeps a key’s existing expiry, so the counter expires on schedule however many times it’s incremented. Calling incr() alone would create a counter that never expires.
The window number is in the key. A new window means a new key, so no reset is needed, and there’s no race where one request resets the counter while another increments it.
The expiry is two windows long, so a counter can’t expire while its window is still current. Expired counters are cleaned up by expire() or eviction like any other entry.

In a real app, use time.time() and leave out clock=; the fake clock is only here so the example can jump to the next minute.


Using it in a view
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException, Request

app = FastAPI()

@app.get('/api/search')
def search(request: Request, q: str) -> dict:
    if not allow_request(request.client.host, limit=100, window=60):
        raise HTTPException(status_code=429, detail='Too many requests')
    return run_search(q)


Things to know

Fixed windows allow short bursts at the boundary. A client can make 100 requests at the end of one minute and 100 more at the start of the next. For most APIs that’s fine. If it isn’t, check both the current and the previous window and weight the previous one by how much of it overlaps the last 60 seconds (a sliding-window estimate).
It’s per machine. Every worker on one machine shares the count, but two machines behind a load balancer each have their own. The planned network server will share one cache across machines.
Fail open on a busy cache. If you set a short timeout on the cache so that requests never wait long, catch Timeout and allow the request rather than failing it:

from diskcache_oxide import Timeout

try:
    allowed = allow_request(client)
except Timeout:
    allowed = True

Don’t rate limit with a cache that might be a NullCache. Its incr() always returns default + delta, so every request would be allowed. That’s often what you want with caching switched off, but make it a deliberate choice.

A ready-made throttle recipe is planned (see the roadmap).

title: diskcache-oxide
text:
diskcache-oxide
A shared, durable disk cache for Python, with a Rust engine, SQLite storage, and a diskcache-compatible API.
Python cache. Rust engine. SQLite storage.
Every Python web app arrives at the same crossroads. A query that was fine at launch is now the slowest thing on the page, so you cache its result in a dict, and for one afternoon you’re a hero. Then the app goes under gunicorn with four workers, and there are four dicts, each warming up alone and each forgetting everything the moment its worker is recycled. So you reach for Redis, and now there’s a server to deploy, secure, monitor and pay for, whose entire job is to remember the answer to one query.
python-diskcache showed there was a third road: a cache that is just a directory. Every thread and every process on the machine opens the same path and sees the same entries, and the entries are still there tomorrow, because a directory doesn’t restart. No daemon, no network hop, no second system to keep alive. It’s the kind of idea that sounds too simple to be fast, and for years that was the catch.
diskcache-oxide removes the catch. It keeps the diskcache API you already know and rebuilds everything beneath it for where Python is going: many cores, many worker processes, free-threaded CPython, and async frameworks that can’t afford a slow call on the event loop. The engine is Rust. The storage is SQLite. The Python layer is as thin as it can be. One thread gets more than 600,000 cache operations a second out of a Cache, eight threads sharing it still get that rate while the defunct python-diskcache’s falls below 20,000, nothing on your disk is a pickle unless you asked for one, and memory and disk use stay where you set them.
Source on GitHub: https://github.com/mikeckennedy/diskcache-oxide · Issues
Here is the whole idea on one screen. Four workers, one directory. The cache makes the slow query cheap, and add() elects exactly one worker to run the hourly job, because a write that’s atomic across processes is a lock if you squint:
And here is what it does under load. Every thread shares one cache, the x axis adds threads, and the two libraries go in opposite directions:

title: diskcache-oxide
text:
Where this is going
diskcache-oxide is being built in three stages. The first is the one you can use today.

A better diskcache. The Cache you already know, rebuilt in Rust: about half the read latency, many times the threaded throughput, safe across fork(), safe on free-threaded Python, and no pickle by default. This is the core that exists now.
The complete local caching toolkit. A native AsyncCache for FastAPI, Litestar and friends, memoize, tags, more eviction policies, Deque and Index, and the coordination recipes (locks, semaphores, throttles, stampede protection) that make a shared cache useful as more than a cache. Two pieces of this stage arrived early: FanoutCache sharding for apps with many writing processes, and transact().
A cache server. The same Rust engine served over the network: a Redis-style central cache for a fleet of machines, with SQLite underneath instead of RAM. As the only owner of its files, the server can use SQLite’s exclusive locking mode, which already measures about 40% faster reads than the shared-directory library.

See Vision and roadmap for how each stage breaks down.

title: diskcache-oxide
text:
Why diskcache-oxide

Fast where web apps spend their time. At a 99:1 read/write mix, one thread gets about 650,000 operations a second from a Cache, 1.6× the defunct diskcache’s rate and cheap enough to call straight from the event loop. Add threads and the gap opens: at 8 threads on a GIL build, diskcache’s per-thread connections pile into each other and its throughput falls to 19,000 a second, while oxide’s stays at 650,000, 34× ahead (the chart above).
Built for free-threaded Python. The extension is compiled with gil_used = false and never leans on the GIL for correctness, which matters on a build where there’s no GIL to lean on. Every change is tested on 3.14, 3.14t, 3.15 and 3.15t.
Safe across fork(). gunicorn, Celery’s prefork pool and multiprocessing create workers by copying the parent, and the copy includes whatever SQLite lock a thread was holding at that instant. A process-wide fork barrier makes sure no child is ever born holding half a transaction.
No pickle on your disk. Values are msgpack (or JSON) with exact type tags, so tuples, sets, datetimes, dates, Decimals, big ints and NaN come back as what you stored, not as whatever the format could manage. Your own types are registered once and read back only where the name is registered. Pickle is opt-in, and a cache that didn’t opt in refuses to unpickle anything it finds, however it got there.
Predictable memory and disk. A bounded connection pool, a 1 MiB page cache per connection, a write-ahead log that trims itself back down, and a checkpoint() for when you want it empty now.
Correct under pressure. clear() never deletes writes that landed while it ran, expire() removes every expired entry, and a reader racing an overwrite gets the old value or the new one, never a spurious miss. Each of these is a bug in diskcache, found by running the same test suite against both libraries, with a reproduction in the repo.
A real off switch. NullCache turns caching off without a single if cache is not None: in your code, and can keep forwarding invalidations to the real cache while it’s off, so nothing stale is waiting when you turn it back on.
Named caches with an off switch. Caches registers an app’s caches once, opens each on first use, hands out a NullCache while one can’t open, and gives an admin page its counts and sizes.
Errors you can act on. Every exception says what went wrong, in words, and the errors page says what to do about it. Nothing is swallowed unless you turned on the setting that swallows it.
Typed. Ships py.typed and a CacheLike protocol that Cache, FanoutCache and NullCache all satisfy.

A conformance suite runs the same tests against real diskcache 5.6.3, so every difference is a decision written down in Divergences, never an accident. Install
pip install diskcache-oxide
It supports CPython 3.14 and 3.15, including the free-threaded builds (3.14t and 3.15t), on macOS and Linux. Anywhere else pip builds from source, which needs the latest stable Rust toolchain. Windows support is planned.
During 0.x, a release that changes the on-disk format bumps the minor version and says so first in its changelog entry: delete existing caches when you upgrade to it. Until you do, opening one raises FormatMismatchError. It’s a cache, so the cost is a cold start.

from diskcache_oxide import Cache

cache = Cache('/var/cache/my-app-oxide')

title: Caches: named caches
text:
Every app with two caches eventually grows a file called something like cache_service.py. It maps names to directories, opens each cache once and hands out the same object afterwards, carries on with caching switched off when a directory can’t be opened, lets you turn one off for a load test, and feeds counts and sizes to an admin page. It’s the same file in every app, written slightly differently each time. Caches is that file, so you don’t have to write it again.
from diskcache_oxide import Caches

caches = Caches('/var/cache/my-app', timeout=1.0, on_decode_error='miss')
caches.register('general')
caches.register('pages', size_limit=2 * 2**30)

caches['general'].set('greeting', 'hello')
caches['pages'].get('/about')
Settings passed to Caches apply to every cache, and register can override them for one. Each cache lives in a directory named after it under the base directory, unless you pass directory=.
One setting works differently here: a function passed as on_decode_error is called as report(name, key, exc), with the cache’s name first, so one reporter can serve every cache. (On a plain Cache it’s report(key, exc).) A function that doesn’t take three arguments is rejected when you create the registry or register the cache.

Lookups
A cache opens on its first lookup, and every lookup after that returns the same object. A lookup is a single dict read with no lock, so it’s fine to do on every request rather than keeping your own references. Lookups are safe from any thread, on free-threaded Python too, and in a child process after a fork.
Caches is generic in its names. Give it a Literal and a misspelled name becomes a type error:
from typing import Literal

CacheName = Literal['general', 'pages']
caches: Caches[CacheName] = Caches('/var/cache/my-app')
caches['genral']  # ty: invalid argument


When a cache can’t open
A cache can fail to open: a permissions problem, a disk that went away, a database written by a newer version, or another process holding the lock for longer than timeout. A lookup then returns a NullCache instead of raising, so the request carries on without the cache. The error goes to on_open_error(name, exc), which logs it at ERROR on the diskcache_oxide logger by default. Pass your own function to send it to Sentry or your logging setup.
The failure is remembered for retry_open_after seconds (10 by default), so a broken cache costs one failed open every 10 seconds, not one per request, and the lookup after that tries again. A cache that recovers is picked up without a restart. Under load, several threads may make that retry at the same moment, and each one that fails reports it.
MemoryError isn’t an open failure, so it raises from the lookup, as it would from Cache(...). That includes SQLite running out of memory while opening (SQLITE_NOMEM), which used to be an OSError and got a NullCache.
A Timeout at open means busy, not broken: another process holding the lock, or a first lookup that collided with a fork. It’s remembered for at most 1 second, and the default report is a WARNING with no traceback. A custom on_open_error still gets the exception. Lookups of a cache that’s already open never touch any of this.
A bad setting (size_limit=True, serializer='yaml') is a bug, not an outage, so it raises on lookup instead. What each open error means, and the fix, is in Errors and what to do about them.


Sharded caches
Pass shards= to register to open a FanoutCache instead of a Cache. It takes the same settings, and max_connections is then a total across the shards.
caches.register('rate_limits', shards=8)
caches.fanout('rate_limits').incr('ip:203.0.113.7')
A plain cache is read with caches[name] and a sharded one with caches.fanout(name), typed FanoutCache | NullCache, because its transact takes a key. Reading a name the wrong way raises TypeError. Passing shards at all picks the kind, even shards=None, so a config file that writes shards: null for “none” would register a FanoutCache: leave it out. A directory that holds the other kind of cache fails to open with LayoutMismatchError, and the lookup returns a NullCache like any failed open.
A sharded cache keeps the shard count it was created with. register('rate_limits', shards=16) on a folder that already has 8 shards opens it with 8, logs a WARNING saying so and how to apply 16, and logs one ERROR per process so an error tracker hears of it. Every process then routes keys by the same count, so a deploy that changes shards= keeps working while old and new workers overlap. The registered count applies only to a new folder: to change it, delete the folder with every worker stopped, for example at deploy. A folder deleted while old workers still run is re-created by whichever process opens it first, with that process’s count. One case is still a NullCache: a size_limit or max_connections that fits the registered count but is too small to split over the folder’s count (at least one connection and 1 MiB a shard) fails with LayoutMismatchError naming both counts. A setting that’s wrong for the registered count itself still raises ValueError from the lookup, as any bad setting does. A direct FanoutCache(path, shards=16) on that folder still raises LayoutMismatchError: only the registry is lenient. Everything else on this page (disable, stats, clear, expire_all, close_all) works the same for both kinds.


Switching caches off
caches.disable('pages')   # later lookups return NullCache(invalidate=real)
caches.enable('pages')
caches.enabled('pages')   # False while it's off
While a cache is disabled, its lookups return NullCache(invalidate=real): reads miss and writes are dropped, but delete and clear still reach the real cache, so entries you invalidate by removing them aren’t served stale when it comes back on. Invalidating by writing doesn’t survive: an overwriting set or a version-bump incr is dropped like any other write, and the old value is served again (see Keep invalidating while caching is off). Switches only change later lookups. Code that already holds the real Cache keeps using it, so set them at startup, before you hand caches out.
If your app has its own names for what it caches (Talk Python calls them purposes), map them onto registered caches in your own code. It’s a few lines:
PURPOSES = {'rss_feed': 'general', 'episode_html': 'episodes'}
off = {'rss_feed'}  # from your settings file

def cache_for(purpose: str) -> CacheLike:
    real = caches[PURPOSES[purpose]]
    return NullCache(invalidate=real) if purpose in off else real
Build the wrapper on each call rather than memoizing it: caches[...] is already cheap, and a memoized NullCache(invalidate=...) wrapped around a cache that had failed to open would never pick up its recovery.


Admin and shutdown
caches.stats()                      # {name: CacheStats(name, directory, enabled, count, volume, error)}
caches.clear('pages', timeout=10)   # works on a disabled cache too
caches.expire_all(timeout=10)       # {name: removed, or None if it failed}
caches.close_all()                  # at shutdown; `with Caches(...) as caches:` does it too

stats() opens every registered cache and never raises: a cache that can’t be read has its error set.
clear(name) raises if the cache can’t be opened, so an admin page doesn’t report “0 cleared” for a failure.
expire_all() runs every cache, logging and reporting None for one that fails. Run it from a scheduled job rather than inside a request: a large expire takes seconds.
Maintenance calls hold the write lock once per chunk, so give them a longer timeout= than the request path’s.



Coming from your own diskcache wrapper
Apps that run diskcache in production tend to grow the same wrapper around it: a class that turns errors into misses, a null cache for turning caching off, and a module that creates, lists and maintains the app’s caches. Talk Python’s, for one, are a DurableCache class and a cache_service module, and the left column uses their names. Each piece now has a home in the library:



A typical wrapper
diskcache-oxide




bool() is always True
Cache is always truthy (D-009); NullCache is falsy


CacheProtocol
CacheLike


NullCache, PerfTestNullCache
NullCache, and NullCache(invalidate=real)


get that logs, deletes and misses on any error
Cache(on_decode_error='miss') or a reporting function (details)


A cache that can’t take a request down
Caches(base_dir, durable=True), which also covers set, whose failures such a wrapper usually raises (details)


create_cache(name, size_limit)
caches.register(name, size_limit=...), then caches[name]


timeout=1.0 on every open
Caches(base_dir, timeout=1.0)


A NullCache when opening fails
the same, reported through on_open_error and retried after 10 s


get_all_caches(), clear_*(), close_all_caches()
caches.stats(), caches.clear(name, timeout=...), caches.close_all()


A separate maintenance handle with a 10 s timeout
timeout= on clear(), expire() and cull()


Hourly expire_all_caches() inside create_cache
caches.expire_all() from a scheduled job



The library’s self-healing read is safer than the wrapper’s in three ways:

It deletes only what failed. The wrapper’s get-then-delete can remove a fresh value another process wrote in between. The library deletes exactly the stored version it couldn’t read.
It never waits to clean up. If the write lock is busy, the bad row stays and a later read tries again.
It doesn’t hide outages. The wrapper catches every exception, so a lock Timeout also became a silent miss. In the library, Timeout, I/O errors and MemoryError still raise by default, and so does reading a pickled value from a cache without pickle=True, which is a configuration mistake. durable=True is how you choose a miss for an outage, and it counts each one and logs them, at most once a minute, rather than staying silent; MemoryError and that mistake raise regardless.

What stays in the app: reading its settings file and environment variables (pass the result as base_dir), its purposes and their on/off flags, descriptions for the admin page, and wiring the reporting functions to Sentry or logbook.

title: Performance
text:
A microsecond is nothing until you multiply it. Web apps call their cache on almost every request, often straight from the asyncio event loop, where every microsecond the cache spends is a microsecond every other request on that loop waits. So diskcache-oxide’s performance work starts with read latency, then throughput under many threads, then predictable resource use. Correctness always comes first: every speedup has to keep the conformance suite green, or it doesn’t ship. The numbers below are the ones that survived.

The numbers
Measured with bench/gate.py, which runs the defunct python-diskcache (5.6.3, its last release, from August 2023) and diskcache-oxide in the same session on the same machine, in four interleaved rounds. These numbers come from Linux (Ubuntu 26.04 LTS) in a container on an Apple Silicon Mac. Both libraries ran in the same container, so the ratios compare like with like, but the absolute numbers on an x86-64 server will differ. Latencies are p50 in microseconds. Ratios are oxide’s time divided by diskcache’s, so lower is better.









Workload
3.14
3.14t (free-threaded)




get, small value, hit
0.76 µs (0.42×)
0.75 µs (0.46×)


get, miss
0.65 µs (0.45×)
0.62 µs (0.46×)

1.18 µs (0.47×)
1.26 µs (0.54×)

2.21 µs (0.65×)
2.41 µs (0.79×)


set, small value
22.6 µs (0.77×)
24.0 µs (0.82×)




Threaded throughput, every thread sharing one Cache, in operations per second at 1/2/4/8 threads (ratios are oxide’s throughput over diskcache’s, so higher is better):









Mix
3.14
3.14t (free-threaded)




99:1 reads to writes
750k / 745k / 723k / 723k (2.0-16.5×)
701k / 639k / 680k / 729k (1.7-1.8×)


1,000:1 reads to writes
900k / 886k / 876k / 875k (2.1-18.9×)
903k / 680k / 1,181k / 1,416k (1.25-2.2×)




Two things stand out:

On GIL builds, diskcache collapses as threads are added and oxide doesn’t. At 99:1, diskcache drops from about 375k to 44k operations per second going from 1 to 8 threads; oxide stays flat around 720-750k. diskcache’s per-thread connections end up fighting over the GIL and SQLite’s locks.
On free-threaded builds, oxide is faster at every thread count, but it doesn’t scale yet. 8 threads reach about 1.4M operations per second at 1,000:1, only 1.6× one thread. That’s the next target, below.

Run them yourself with python -m bench.gate. Numbers vary by machine; the ratios are what the gate enforces.


Where the speed comes from

Rust from the call to the disk. A get goes from Python straight into compiled Rust: one prepared SQLite statement, decode, done. There’s no Python wrapper in between.
Statements prepared once. Each pooled connection caches its prepared statements, so a lookup never recompiles SQL.
The clock is read in Rust. Checking expiry doesn’t call back into Python’s time.time().
Fast codecs. msgpack and tagged JSON are encoded and decoded in Rust, building Python objects directly.
Reads never write. Least-recently-stored eviction means a get never updates anything, so any number of readers proceed in parallel.
A smarter write lock. Writers in one process queue on an in-process lock per database file, instead of every thread retrying against SQLite’s busy handler.
SQLite tuned for it. The bundled SQLite is built with its global memory statistics turned off, which removes a process-wide mutex from every allocation: 2-10% more threaded throughput.



Prefix scans at scale
diskcache’s iterkeys() gets slower faster than the cache grows: about 1.7 seconds at 100,000 keys, and over 25 seconds at 400,000. diskcache-oxide’s iterkeys(prefix=...) is an indexed range scan, paged in batches so no read transaction is held between them. 400,000 keys scan in about 10 ms.


Memory that stays flat
Memory is bounded by configuration, not by how many threads touch the cache: at most max_connections connections per database file (default 8), each with a 1 MiB page cache. A FanoutCache defaults to two per shard for the whole root, about 16 MiB at 8 shards. A separate memory-instrumented build runs bench/memory.py and the memory tests under heavy load to hold that bound. See Storage and WAL.


Known slow spots
Two oversubscribed cases measure slower than before the SQLite mutex spin and the connection-slot spin went in. Both are known, and neither is in the path of a web app running a few threads per process.

A plain Cache with far more threads than cores, all sharing one handle: 7% slower on an M-series Mac at 36 threads, and 5% in a Linux VM at 32. Faster hand-off lets more threads into SQLite at once.
A FanoutCache at max_connections=32 with 8 threads, on macOS only: 5-12% slower. The same case on Linux is 41-56% faster.



Next: free-threaded scaling
Profiling a cached get shows that about 60% of its time is one system call: SQLite taking its shared-memory read lock on the -shm file, under a process-wide mutex. It’s the biggest single cost on every read, and it’s also what keeps free-threaded throughput from scaling. The next stage goes after it, along with:

a per-process lock-caching layer under SQLite, or longer-lived read snapshots;
thread-affine connections;
cheaper reference counting on shared Cache objects in free-threaded builds;
Making threads that share one handle scale. FanoutCache is built and removes the multi-process write-lock ceiling, but at its default settings it doesn’t lift this read ceiling, so the shared per-handle path is being worked on.

Past that, the network server can go further still: as the only owner of its files, it can use SQLite’s exclusive locking mode, which keeps that lock in ordinary memory. Measured reads drop from 1.18 µs to 0.69 µs.

title: Switching from python-diskcache
text:
If you’re here, the question is a practical one: what breaks? Very little, and on purpose. diskcache-oxide is API compatible with python-diskcache 5.6.3’s Cache, and deliberately not data compatible. Keeping diskcache’s API makes switching a one-line change. Not keeping its on-disk format is what made it possible to fix the design instead of inheriting it, pickle and all. So the switch itself is small, and the rest of this page is about what you’ll notice afterwards, which is mostly things getting better and now and then things getting stricter.
For most apps, switching looks like this:

title: Switching from python-diskcache
text:
Upgrading diskcache-oxide
During 0.x, a release that changes the on-disk format bumps the minor version and says so first in its changelog entry. Delete existing caches when you upgrade to it, with every worker stopped. Until you do, opening one raises FormatMismatchError, which a Caches registry reports and answers with a NullCache. A release that keeps the format needs nothing.

title: Errors and what to do about them
text:
Sooner or later a traceback ends in diskcache_oxide, and the question is whether it’s your bug, an outage, or two processes disagreeing about what a directory is for. diskcache-oxide raises when something is wrong rather than guessing, and each exception is chosen so that except clauses you already have keep working: Timeout is a TimeoutError, TransactionAborted is a RuntimeError, UnsafeValueError is a TypeError, LayoutMismatchError is a ValueError. This page is the field guide: every exception, what it means, and what to do. The last section covers the log lines the library writes when it has been told not to raise, because then a log line is the only evidence you’ll get.








Exception
Base classes
Where




Timeout
TimeoutError (so OSError)
any call that waits for a lock or a fork


TransactionBusy
Timeout
transact() on a second cache


TransactionAborted
RuntimeError
a transact() block that didn’t commit


UnsafeValueError
TypeError
reading a pickled value without pickle=True


CorruptValueError
ValueError
reading a value no build could decode


ForeignValueError
CorruptValueError
reading a value another version or host could decode


FormatMismatchError
RuntimeError
opening a database or manifest this version can’t read


LayoutMismatchError
FormatMismatchError, ValueError
opening a directory as the wrong kind of cache


TypeError, ValueError, KeyError, RuntimeError, OSError, MemoryError
built-in
described below




TypeError at set(): a value that can’t be stored
TypeError: values of type Episode can't be stored without pickle (only exact built-in types round-trip)
The value isn’t one the msgpack or JSON format can represent exactly, so it’s refused where it was created rather than three requests later when something reads it. Only exact built-in types round-trip: str, bytes, int, float, bool, None, and list, tuple, dict, set and datetime made of those. A dataclass, an ORM row, a dict subclass or a class of your own doesn’t.
Fix it in this order:

Register the type: diskcache_oxide.register_type(Episode, name='tp.Episode') for a dataclass, or with encode= and decode= functions for anything else (an ObjectId, a namedtuple, a str subclass). The value is stored without pickle and comes back as the type you stored. See Your own types.
Or store a plain structure instead: a dict from a model’s model_dump(), and rebuild the object on the way out.
If you really need arbitrary objects, open a separate cache for them with Cache('/var/cache/my-app-objects', pickle=True). Don’t turn pickle=True on for a cache that other code shares just to make the error go away: every reader of that directory then runs pickle.loads on whatever is written there. See Serialization.

A registered type that still raises here is one whose encode function raised, or returned something the codec can’t store, or a dataclass with a field it can’t store. That raises even on a cache with pickle=True: a registered type is never pickled.


TypeError for keys and booleans
TypeError: cache keys must be str, not int
TypeError: expire must be a number of seconds or None, not bool
Keys are str only for now; build them yourself (f'user:{user_id}'). Other key types are planned and won’t need a format change. A bool where a number of seconds belongs (expire=True, timeout=True) is almost always an argument in the wrong position, so it’s refused rather than treated as 1, which is what diskcache does.


Timeout: a lock or a fork outlasted timeout
diskcache_oxide.Timeout: timed out after 1 s waiting for a lock or a pending fork
The call waited the cache’s timeout (60 s by default, or the timeout= passed to that call) and gave up. Something held what it needed, and there are three suspects:

Another writer held the write lock that long. One process at a time commits to a database file, and a burst of writes, a clear() from a maintenance script, or a long transact() block holds it. Reads never wait for writers, so a Timeout on a get is one of the next two cases.
A fork was pending. Before a fork, every cache call in the process waits for in-flight writes and then for the fork itself, and that counts against timeout. A fork takes about a millisecond in a quiet process and tens to hundreds of milliseconds beside busy threads on a GIL build. A timeout below that sees Timeout during ordinary forks. See How long a call waits for a fork.
Reading a large value kept losing to overwrites of the same key until timeout. Rare, and only on a key that’s rewritten flat out.

What to do:

In a request path, catch it and skip the cache. Give the cache a short timeout (Cache(path, timeout=1.0)), and treat Timeout as “don’t cache this time”: the value is a copy, and the request can go to the source of truth. Sharing a cache across web workers has the pattern.
Give maintenance its own timeout. clear(), expire() and cull() take timeout= for that call, and bound each chunk’s wait, so an admin page can pass clear(timeout=10) on a cache whose requests use 1 second. Run them from one scheduled job rather than from every worker.
Keep transact() blocks short, and never await inside one.
If many processes write often, use a FanoutCache. A plain Cache has one write lock per directory, and eight workers that all write queue on it. Sharding gives each shard its own.
Let the library answer it as a miss with durable=True: single-key calls then return their miss value instead of raising, and the failure is counted and logged. Pair it with a small timeout, since it doesn’t bound time on its own.
checkpoint() never raises Timeout: it returns False when other processes keep it busy. Call it again later, or at shutdown.



TransactionBusy: two caches in one transaction
Inside one cache’s transact() block, beginning a transaction on a second cache whose write lock another thread holds raises TransactionBusy at once instead of waiting. That thread could be waiting for the lock you hold, and then neither would ever finish. It’s a Timeout subclass, so existing handlers catch it, and retry=True never retries it.
Nest the two caches in the same order everywhere in your app. When TransactionBusy reaches you, leave the outer block, so your lock is released, and try the whole thing again. See Transactions.


TransactionAborted: a block that didn’t commit
TransactionAborted: the write transaction was rolled back after an error; nothing in it can commit
A with cache.transact(): block never exits cleanly when its writes are gone. This one comes from a write inside the block, or from the block’s exit, after one of its operations failed in a way that left the transaction unusable (a full disk, an I/O error).
TransactionAborted: the transaction did not commit: another thread or an earlier exit ended it, or it was rolled back after an error
This one comes from the block’s exit, when the transaction had already ended without committing: another thread rolled it back, or an earlier __exit__ call on the same object ended it (including one made from inside the block’s own operations, such as a pickle hook, which raises RuntimeError where it’s called and rolls the transaction back when that operation returns).
Either way nothing in the block was kept. Treat it as you would the original failure: log it, and run the block again if the work is idempotent. TransactionAborted is a RuntimeError, so an except RuntimeError you already have still catches it; catch TransactionAborted to handle this case alone.


RuntimeError from a transaction
RuntimeError: this database can't be written in a process forked inside a transaction
A process forked while the forking thread itself held a transact() block, and this is the child. The parent’s transaction carries on and commits; the child’s copy is poisoned, and its writes to that database raise this instead of stalling for a minute. Don’t fork from inside a transaction: start worker processes before the block, or after it. See Forking from inside your own transaction.


UnsafeValueError: a pickled value, read without pickle=True
UnsafeValueError: this value was stored with pickle; open the cache with pickle=True to read it
Two openers of one directory disagree about what it’s allowed to hold. A handle opened without pickle=True found a row that a pickle=True handle wrote, and refused to unpickle it, because unpickling runs whatever code the bytes describe. The row is left in place for the handle that can read it. This is a configuration mismatch, not damage, so it raises under every on_decode_error policy and under durable=True too.
Decide which the directory is for. If it holds pickled objects on purpose, open every handle on it with pickle=True. If it shouldn’t, find the writer that passed pickle=True and give it its own directory, then clear() this one. It’s a TypeError, like the error at set() above, because both come from the same decision: what this cache is allowed to hold.


CorruptValueError and ForeignValueError: a value that can’t be decoded
ForeignValueError: ...
CorruptValueError: ...
CorruptValueError means no build of diskcache-oxide could read the stored bytes: they’re malformed, a pickled class has been removed since it was stored, or a registered type’s decode function raised about the row (a dataclass row written before a field was removed, say), in which case your exception is its __cause__. ForeignValueError, its subclass, means this build can’t read them but another might: a newer version wrote a mode or tag this one doesn’t know, the value needs a time zone this host doesn’t have, or it holds a registered type this process hasn’t registered (the message names the tag: register it, at import time).
By default a read raises these, as diskcache does. A cache holds copies, so most apps would rather treat them as a miss:

Cache(..., on_decode_error='miss') returns the default, logs a warning on the diskcache_oxide logger, and deletes a row no build could read. A foreign row is kept, since the build that wrote it can still read it. durable=True turns this on by default.
Pass a function instead to report it yourself: on_decode_error=lambda key, exc: sentry.capture(exc). From a Caches registry it’s called as (name, key, exc).
For a ForeignValueError that keeps coming back, upgrade the older readers to the version that wrote the value, or stop the newer writer from sharing the directory. For a missing time zone, install the host’s zone data.

The full table of what each policy does with each failure is in Values that can’t be read.


FormatMismatchError: a database this version can’t read
FormatMismatchError: cache format version 3 is not supported (this build uses version 2) at /var/cache/my-app
The directory holds a database, or a FanoutCache manifest, written in a format this build doesn’t know, usually by a newer diskcache-oxide. Nothing is read or changed. Upgrade this process to match the writer, or point it at a different directory. If the directory should be reset, stop every process using it and delete it; a cache starts cold without harm.


LayoutMismatchError: the wrong kind of cache for the directory
LayoutMismatchError: the root has 8 shards, not 16
The directory’s layout doesn’t match how it was opened: a plain Cache on a FanoutCache root or one of its shard directories, a FanoutCache on a plain Cache’s directory, or a shards= count that differs from the one the root records. The refused open creates nothing, so a typo doesn’t leave a directory neither kind can open. It’s both a ValueError and a FormatMismatchError.
Use the class the directory was created with, and for a FanoutCache either leave shards out (the stored count is used) or pass the stored one. A different shard count means a new directory: the count decides where every key lives, so it can’t change in place. See The layout and the hash. In a Caches registry, a lookup that hits a role mismatch returns a NullCache and reports it like any failed open. Another shard count is not an error there: the registry opens the folder with the count on disk and logs a warning (below). It still fails with LayoutMismatchError, and so a NullCache, when a size_limit or max_connections that fits the registered count is too small to split over the folder’s count; delete the folder or raise the setting.


RuntimeError: the filesystem can’t run SQLite in WAL mode
RuntimeError: the cache requires WAL journal mode, but SQLite is using "delete"
SQLite refused write-ahead logging, which diskcache-oxide requires for readers and a writer to work at the same time. That happens on network filesystems (NFS, SMB) and some FUSE mounts. The cache has to live on a local disk: /var/cache/<app>, or a Docker volume on the host’s disk. See Pick a directory.


OSError

Too many open files (errno EMFILE) opening a FanoutCache. Each shard takes about 4 file descriptors to open, so 256 shards need more than Linux’s usual ulimit -n of 1,024. The message gives the shard count, the descriptors needed, the limit and how many are already open. Raise the limit, or use fewer shards; eight is plenty for most apps. A failed open leaves nothing behind.
No hard links. Creating a FanoutCache manifest uses a hard link, so a filesystem without them (FAT, exFAT, SMB, some FUSE mounts) raises OSError saying so. Use a local disk.
Disk full, or an I/O error. The write didn’t happen and the cache is unchanged. Under durable=True a single-key call answers it as a miss or False and logs it; otherwise it raises. Timeout is an OSError too, so an except OSError around a cache call catches both.



ValueError

size_limit below 1 MiB. In diskcache a tiny limit silently evicts every value, including the one just stored; here it’s refused. For a FanoutCache the total must be at least shards MiB, since each shard needs 1 MiB.
max_connections below shards on a FanoutCache. Each shard needs at least one connection.
A key on another shard inside transact(key=...). The block covers one shard, and a call for a key elsewhere, reads included, can’t be atomic with it. Check with shard_of() that the keys share a shard, or keep them in one value.
A Caches name that’s taken, isn’t a plain directory name, or would share a directory with another registered cache.



KeyError

cache[key] and del cache[key] for a missing or expired key, as with a dict. Use get() and delete() for the “might not be there” cases.
incr(key, default=None) and decr(key, default=None) on a missing key. With the default default=0, a missing key starts counting from 0 instead.
Every NullCache[key], since nothing is ever present.



MemoryError
It always raises, under durable=True too, including when SQLite runs out of memory. A Caches lookup raises it as well, rather than handing out a NullCache.


Log lines, when the library was told not to raise
Three settings turn failures into log lines on the diskcache_oxide logger instead of exceptions. Make sure that logger reaches your logging setup, since the line is then the only signal.

on_decode_error='miss' logs a warning for each stored version it couldn’t read, once per cache handle, and deletes the row if no build could read it.
durable=True counts every swallowed failure in one of three groups and logs each group’s first failure at once, then at most once a minute per cache handle, with counts by operation since its last line (get: 1204, set: 37). Busy (a Timeout) logs at WARNING, failing (a full disk, an I/O error, a damaged database) at ERROR, and lost invalidations (any failed delete, whose entry can now be served stale) at ERROR. An outage that ends within the minute shows only its first failure until the next line, so each line says more may follow. close() logs what’s left.
Caches logs could not open cache 'pages' at /var/cache/my-app/pages; using a NullCache, retrying in 10 s at ERROR with the traceback when a cache can’t open, and the same at WARNING without one when the open merely timed out (that’s retried after at most 1 s). Pass on_open_error= to send it to Sentry instead.
Caches also logs cache 'rate_limits' at /var/cache/my-app/rate_limits has 8 shards but is registered with shards=16; using the 8 on disk. To apply shards=16, delete /var/cache/my-app/rate_limits while no process has it open at WARNING each time it opens a sharded cache whose folder has another count than the registration, and once per process a FanoutCache is registered with a shard count its folder does not have at ERROR, a constant message with the details in the record’s cache, directory, stored_shards and registered_shards attributes, so an error tracker groups every worker’s report into one issue. The cache works throughout; this one doesn’t go through on_open_error, since the open succeeded.



If it looks like a bug in diskcache-oxide
If you’ve read this far and the traceback still doesn’t fit, it may be one. Open an issue with diskcache_oxide.__version__, diskcache_oxide.sqlite_version(), the interpreter (python -VV says whether it’s free-threaded), the platform and filesystem, how many processes and threads share the directory, and the full traceback. Every deliberate difference from diskcache is listed in Divergences, so check there first if the surprise is a behavior rather than an error.
