title: Concurrency and forks
text: A production Python web app is a crowd. Several worker processes, often several threads in each, a pre-forking server that creates and recycles those workers while they’re busy, and a cron job or an admin script opening the same cache on the side. More and more, it’s also free-threaded Python, where the threads really do run at the same time. diskcache-oxide is designed for all of that at once, and its test suite runs each of these cases on every change, because this is where cache bugs hide: not in get and set, but in what happens when two of them collide.

title: Concurrency and forks
text:
A bounded connection pool
diskcache opens a SQLite connection for every thread that touches the cache and keeps it. With 64 threads that’s 131 open files in the cache directory, and a server with enough threads runs out of file descriptors.
diskcache-oxide shares a pool of connections per database file across every handle in the process:
cache = Cache('/var/cache/my-app', max_connections=8)   # the default
The pool never holds more than max_connections connections, so at most 2 × max_connections + 1 files are open in the cache directory, however many threads you run. A thread that finds every connection busy waits for one, up to the cache’s timeout. When the last handle on a directory closes, every connection closes with it, whichever threads used them.

title: Concurrency and forks
section: How long a call waits for a fork
text:
How long a call waits for a fork
A fork counts against timeout. A cache call behind a pending fork waits for it through the call’s own timeout and then raises Timeout, so timeout has to exceed the work in flight, plus the fork, plus the interpreter hand-off. A fork takes about a millisecond in a quiet small process, but tens to hundreds of milliseconds beside busy threads on a GIL build (the forking thread has to get the interpreter back), longer in a large process, and it waits for work in flight such as a forced checkpoint. A timeout under that sees Timeout during ordinary forks, and a loop on timeout=0 adds to the problem by being one of those busy threads.
A fork waits for every transaction another thread holds, with no timeout of its own, so a long transaction delays every fork in the process. Code that holds a transaction or runs inside a pickle hook (or a registered type’s decode function, which runs in the same place), and waits for another thread’s cache call, can keep a fork from finishing: the fork waits for that code, and the other thread waits for the fork. That other thread’s call now raises Timeout, and the fork finishes once your code lets go. Until it does, os.fork() doesn’t return, a second os.fork() queues behind it, and every thread with no transaction or hook of its own gets Timeout on every Cache in the process, after using up its whole timeout (60 seconds by default). Other processes aren’t affected. If the code never reacts (a hook that retries forever, or one blocked on something that isn’t a cache call), the fork stays stuck. A hook stuck in C code that holds the GIL stops everything, as it would without a cache.
Two calls don’t raise. checkpoint() returns False when a fork keeps it from running. close() takes at most about 2 seconds behind a stuck fork, 1 for the checkpoint and 1 for the release, and del about 1, whatever timeout is. An ordinary fork ends well inside that, so close() waits it out as usual. If the fork outlasts it, close() returns anyway and the connections close when the fork ends.
Before-fork hooks run in reverse registration order, and logging and concurrent.futures each take a lock in theirs and keep it until the fork is over. diskcache_oxide makes sure its own hook runs before those two, so they stay usable while a fork waits for your code: a pickle hook or a decode function can still log or submit work. Two things it can’t fix. Another library’s hook that takes a lock and is registered after diskcache_oxide stays held while a fork is stuck. And a thread that calls the cache while holding logging’s module lock can hold up a fork until that call’s timeout.
With durable=True, a Timeout behind a fork is a miss or False rather than an exception on a single-key call, so a timeout shorter than this makes ordinary forks into misses. A pickle hook or a registered type’s decode that re-raises the Timeout it got from another thread’s call lets go of its level under any policy, which clears the stuck fork. What durable=True adds is that the request doesn’t fail: that Timeout is a miss, with the row kept.

title: Concurrency and forks
section: Forking from inside your own transaction
text:
Forking from inside your own transaction
CPython won’t let a library refuse a fork, so the barrier can’t wait for a transaction held by the very thread that is forking. The child’s copy of that transaction is poisoned: anything done inside it raises RuntimeError and nothing commits, and the child’s writes to that database raise RuntimeError straight away instead of stalling for a minute. A transact() in the child doesn’t join the inherited transaction either: it raises RuntimeError too. The parent’s block carries on and commits as usual, and the parent gets a RuntimeWarning. A clear error at the call site beats a mysterious 60-second hang in a fresh worker.

title: Serialization
text:
A cache has a quiet second job: it’s a program that reads bytes it didn’t write, left on disk by whatever process got there first. That makes the serializer the most security-relevant piece of the whole library, and it has three jobs. What goes into the cache should come out as exactly what you put in. Encoding and decoding should be fast, because they happen on every call. And reading the cache should never run code that someone else left there. diskcache’s default, pickle, does the first two well and fails the third by design: unpickling runs whatever the bytes tell it to. diskcache-oxide gets all three, and pickle becomes something you opt into, one cache at a time.

Two formats
Each cache picks a structured format with serializer=:
cache = Cache('/var/cache/my-app')                       # msgpack, the default
readable = Cache('/var/cache/my-app-json', serializer='json')

msgpack (the default) is compact and fast. On a 450 KB page-cache entry it’s about 25× faster than tagged JSON, and it stores nested bytes without base64.
json is human-readable: open diskcache-oxide.sqlite in any SQLite browser and read your values. It uses serde_json with exact float round-tripping.

Plain str and bytes values skip both and are stored raw. Every row records how it was encoded, so if you change a cache’s serializer, existing entries stay readable.


Exact types
JSON turns tuples into lists and can’t store sets, datetimes, NaN, very large ints, or dicts with non-str keys. msgpack has some of the same gaps. The usual answer is to coerce quietly and let the bug show up later.
diskcache-oxide’s encoder, written in Rust, notices anything its format would change and tags it instead, so it decodes back to the same type:







Python value
Comes back as




tuple
a tuple, not a list


set
a set


frozenset
a frozenset


datetime.datetime
a datetime, with its timezone and microseconds


datetime.date
a date


decimal.Decimal
a Decimal, exact


int wider than 64 bits
the same int


float('nan'), inf, -inf
the same float


bytes nested in a container
bytes


dict with int (or other non-str) keys
the same keys



import datetime

cache.set('record', {
    'created': datetime.datetime.now(datetime.UTC),
    'point': (37.77, -122.42),
    'ids': {101, 102},
    'big': 2**128,
    'by_id': {1: 'one', 2: 'two'},
})

record = cache.get('record')
assert isinstance(record['point'], tuple)
assert record['by_id'][1] == 'one'
User data can’t be mistaken for a tag: a dict that happens to look like one is escaped on the way in and decoded as an ordinary dict on the way out.


What isn’t stored
A value that neither format can represent exactly, such as an instance of your own class, raises TypeError at set():
cache.set('service', MyService())
# TypeError: values of type MyService can't be stored without pickle (only exact built-in types round-trip)
Only exact built-in types count. A subclass of dict or str isn’t stored as its base type, because it wouldn’t come back as the class you stored. Failing at set() time means you find out where the value was created, not three requests later when something reads it. For a type of your own, or one from a library, register it.


Your own types
Most of what an app stores that isn’t a built-in is a type it doesn’t own: a bson ObjectId inside a session dict, a namedtuple a library hands back, the str subclass a Markdown renderer returns. Converting those by hand at every call site works, but it’s the kind of code that drifts. Instead, tell the codec once how to store the type:
from bson import ObjectId
import diskcache_oxide

diskcache_oxide.register_type(ObjectId, name='bson.ObjectId', encode=str, decode=ObjectId)

cache.set('session', {'id': ObjectId(), 'user': ObjectId()})
cache.get('session')['id']   # an ObjectId again
encode turns an instance into a value the codec can already store, built-ins or other registered types, nested as deep as you like. decode turns that value back into an instance. The registration is process-wide, so make it at import time, in every process that opens the directory.
A dataclass needs only a name. Its init=True fields are read straight off the instance, with no intermediate dict, and on the way out it’s rebuilt with cls(**fields), so defaults and __post_init__ still run:
@dataclasses.dataclass
class Episode:
    id: int
    title: str
    published: datetime.datetime | None = None

diskcache_oxide.register_type(Episode, name='tp.Episode')
cache.set('episode:491', Episode(491, 'Rust and Python'))
The write path skips dataclasses.asdict(), which deep-copies: on a 20-field dataclass a set() goes from about 23 µs to 18. A read still builds one keyword dict and calls the constructor, so it saves almost nothing (4.0 µs against 3.8), and that’s fine: a cache is mostly reads, and what you gain is the call sites.
What the registry guarantees:

Nothing is imported by name. A registered value is stored as {"$t:bson.ObjectId": "..."}, and a reader looks that name up in its own registry. A process that hasn’t registered it gets ForeignValueError, and the row stays for one that has. That is the whole difference from pickle.
The name is yours. Rename or move the class and the stored rows still read, because the tag is the name you chose, not the class’s path.
Lookup is by exact type. A subclass of a registered class is its own registration. The codec’s own types (str, dict, datetime and the rest) can’t be registered, since their wire form is a contract across versions; their subclasses can, which is how a namedtuple or a str subclass gets in.
A registered type is never pickled, even on a cache with pickle=True. Once the encoder has used a registration for any part of a value, that value is stored through it or set() raises: if its encode raises, or returns something the codec can’t store. You registered it to stay off pickle, and a silent fallback would hide the bug.
Last registration wins, by class and by name, so a module that a dev server reloads can register its new class object again.
A decode function’s errors are classified as a pickle hook’s would be. A Timeout or OSError raises with the row kept (a miss under durable=True). An error about the row, such as a TypeError from a dataclass row written before a field was removed, becomes CorruptValueError with yours as __cause__, and on_decode_error='miss' deletes that row so the writer replaces it. Decode runs while the cache holds a connection, as unpickling does, so a slow decode delays forks and checkpoints for as long as it runs; one that re-enters the cache is fine.

A cache that needs a different encoding of a type than the rest of the process gets its own registry, consulted before the global one:
reg = diskcache_oxide.TypeRegistry()
reg.register(ObjectId, name='bson.ObjectId', encode=lambda o: o.binary, decode=ObjectId)
cache = Cache('/var/cache/my-app-binary-ids', types=reg)
Two processes with different registrations on one directory write rows the other can’t read, the same way two processes with different serializer= settings would. Register at import time, the same way everywhere.


Why pickle is off by default

Unpickling runs code. Anyone who can write to the cache directory, including a compromised neighbor process or a shared volume, can make every reader run arbitrary Python.
Pickle hides mistakes. Database sessions, open files and other objects that were never meant to be cached get pickled without complaint and fail later in confusing ways.



Opting in to pickle
When you really do need to cache arbitrary objects, turn pickle on for that cache. It’s used only for values the structured format can’t represent; everything else is still stored as msgpack or JSON.
objects = Cache('/var/cache/my-app-objects', pickle=True)
objects.set('service', MyService())
A good habit is to give pickled values their own cache directory, and keep everything else in a cache without pickle.


Reading safely: UnsafeValueError
Several processes can open one directory with different settings. A handle opened without pickle=True never unpickles. If it reads a value that a pickle=True handle stored, it raises diskcache_oxide.UnsafeValueError (a TypeError subclass) and leaves the row in place, so the pickle=True handle can still read it.
A value whose stored bytes can’t be decoded at all raises CorruptValueError (a ValueError subclass).

title: Storage and WAL
text: Nobody restarts a cache. It sits inside a worker process for weeks, and whatever it does to memory and disk, it does slowly and out of sight, until an alert fires at a bad hour. So how much a cache uses has to be something you set, not something you discover. This page covers what diskcache-oxide puts on disk, and the settings that keep memory and disk where you put them.

title: Storage and WAL
text:
Always on: wal_size_limit
cache = Cache('/var/cache/my-app', wal_size_limit=64 * 1024 * 1024)   # the default
This tells SQLite to trim the log back to half the limit (32 MiB by default) whenever it resets, and scales how often SQLite checkpoints automatically. These are connection settings, so they never pause anything. At normal load they keep the log at a few MiB.

title: Storage and WAL
text:
On demand: checkpoint()
cache.checkpoint()   # True if the log was reset and truncated
checkpoint() copies the log into the database and truncates it to zero. It waits briefly for in-flight reads, retrying up to the cache’s timeout, and returns False instead of raising if other processes keep the database busy. Call it when a short pause suits your app: at shutdown, in a maintenance job, or after a large clear().

title: Storage and WAL
text:
At close
close() runs the same checkpoint when this is the process’s last handle on the cache and the log is over half the limit, waiting at most a second. A small log, the usual case, costs nothing extra. Pass close(checkpoint=False) to skip it.

title: Storage and WAL
text:
Opt-in: automatic checkpoints
cache = Cache('/var/cache/my-app', wal_checkpoint='auto')
With 'auto', writes check the log (at most every 250 ms or 64 writes) and checkpoint it when it’s over the limit, with the interpreter released. Readers in other processes can get in the way for a moment, so it tries the final truncation up to 8 times, a couple of milliseconds each, before backing off for a second. It never fails a write. It isn’t the default because on a saturated disk the write that triggers the checkpoint can still pause for a long time, and no write should pay for housekeeping unless you asked for it. The plan is to move this into a background maintenance thread so writes never pay for it at all. Writes queue behind a checkpoint for tens of milliseconds, so a timeout under about 35 ms can time out behind one.

title: Storage and WAL
section: The limit is a target, not a bound
text:
The limit is a target, not a bound
wal_size_limit says where the log should stay, not where it’s guaranteed to stay. Sustained writes from several processes near flat out can take it to tens of times the limit: we measured 6 GiB on free-threaded 3.15 and 21 GiB on 3.14 in 10 minutes, against a 64 MiB limit. It’s much smaller below flat out, for example 250 MiB at about 2,600 writes per second across 3 writers in auto.
In the default manual mode, with busy readers in other processes, the log grows until something checkpoints. If your app has that shape, use wal_checkpoint='auto' or call checkpoint() periodically. A script should call checkpoint() or close() after a large fill.

title: FanoutCache: sharded caches
text: A plain Cache has one write lock per database file, which makes it a shop with one checkout lane: readers walk straight through, but every writer queues, and eight worker processes that all bump counters are eight carts in one lane. A FanoutCache opens more lanes. It’s one cache spread over several SQLite databases, called shards. Each key lives in exactly one shard, chosen by a fixed hash of the key, so writes to different keys go to different files and stop queueing on one lock. It has the same methods as Cache for single keys, and it’s one directory, shared by any number of threads and processes.

title: FanoutCache: sharded caches
section: Plain Cache and FanoutCache directories don’t mix
text:
Plain Cache and FanoutCache directories don’t mix
A Cache opened on a FanoutCache’s directory, or on one of its shard directories, raises LayoutMismatchError, and so does a FanoutCache opened on a plain Cache’s directory. The refused open creates nothing, so a typo doesn’t leave a directory that neither kind can open. LayoutMismatchError is both a ValueError and a FormatMismatchError. If a registry hits it, the lookup returns a NullCache and reports it like any failed open. A registry that meets another shard count than its registration’s opens the folder with the count on disk and warns instead (Caches).

title: Transactions
text:
Every write is already its own transaction, atomic across every thread and process using the directory. Sometimes one write at a time isn’t enough. A request bumps a total, bumps a per-path counter and records when it happened, and a reader that sees two of those three has seen something that was never true. transact() groups several calls into one: they all commit together when the block exits, or none of them do.
That’s also faster. Each commit costs a disk sync, so grouping writes pays for one instead of several: three counter bumps measured 79 µs one by one and 48 µs in one transaction.

title: Transactions
text:
Two caches at once: TransactionBusy
Inside one cache’s transaction, beginning a transaction on a second cache takes that cache’s write lock if it’s free. If another thread holds it, transact() raises TransactionBusy at once instead of waiting: that thread could be waiting for the lock you hold, and then neither would ever finish. TransactionBusy is a subclass of Timeout, so existing handlers still catch it, and retry=True never retries it, since trying again while you still hold the first lock can’t help.
To use two caches in one block, always nest them in the same order everywhere in your app, and if TransactionBusy reaches you, leave the outer block and try the whole thing again.

title: Transactions
text:
Ending it from another thread
diskcache says a transaction “may not be shared between threads”. In diskcache-oxide, any thread may call the transaction’s __exit__, to commit (no exception) or roll back the owner’s transaction. The rules:

While the owner is inside one of its own operations (decoding a value, say), a rollback is left to that operation, and happens when it returns. A commit waits for it, up to the cache’s timeout. A commit that can’t run by then raises Timeout and rolls back.
The owner’s own exit afterwards raises TransactionAborted unless the transaction committed.
An owner’s exit that comes while the other thread is still committing waits for the outcome, up to the cache’s timeout, and reports it. Past that, it raises Timeout (“whether it committed is unknown”). An exit with an exception passing doesn’t wait.
Writes the owner makes after another thread ended the transaction run on their own, outside it.

title: Vision and roadmap
text:
A shared cache is one of the first pieces of infrastructure a Python web app grows into, and today the choice is awkward. An in-process dict is fast, but each worker has its own copy and it’s gone on restart. Redis is shared and durable, but it’s a separate server, a network hop on every read, and one more thing to run. python-diskcache showed there’s a lot of room between those two: a cache that is just a directory, shared by every thread and process on the machine, built on SQLite.
diskcache-oxide is a bet that this middle option can be much bigger than it has been. With a Rust engine underneath, a directory-backed cache can be fast enough to call on the event loop, safe enough for pre-forking servers and free-threaded Python, and complete enough to cover the jobs people now reach for Redis to do: caching, counters, rate limits, locks, job claims and queues. And when one machine isn’t enough, the same engine can be served over the network.
It’s being built in three stages.


Keep diskcache’s API, fix what’s wrong underneath it, and make it fast. Behavior comes first: every phase keeps a conformance suite green against real diskcache 5.6.3 before chasing speed, and every deliberate difference is written down in Divergences.



Everything diskcache offers that real apps use, plus the things a modern Python stack needs that it never had: an async API, sharding designed for many threads, and coordination recipes that are atomic across every process on the machine.



The same Rust core, served over HTTP to many clients: a Redis-style central cache with SQLite underneath, for when your app outgrows one machine. A server that is the only owner of its files can run SQLite in exclusive locking mode, which keeps the WAL index in heap memory instead of a shared file. title: Getting started
text: A Cache is a directory. That’s the whole mental model, and it carries further than it looks: open the same directory from any number of threads and processes and they all share one cache, nobody has to be told about anybody else, and the entries are still there after a restart, because a directory doesn’t restart. Hold on to that sentence; most of what follows is a consequence of it. This page covers installing diskcache-oxide, the everyday operations, the handful of things that only start to matter once several processes are involved, and how to shut down cleanly.

title: Getting started
text:
Close it, or use with
with Cache('/var/cache/my-app') as cache:
    cache.set('greeting', 'hello')
close() returns the handle’s SQLite connections. Once the last handle on a directory in a process closes, nothing in that directory is held open, so it’s safe to move or delete.

title: Getting started
text:
Dictionary syntax
cache['alpha'] = 100
assert 'alpha' in cache
assert cache['alpha'] == 100
del cache['alpha']        # KeyError if it's missing, like a dict

title: Getting started
text:
Remove values
cache.delete('user:42')             # True if it was there
value = cache.pop('session:7')      # the value, or the default if it was missing

title: Getting started
text:
What a dropped call costs
A failure reaches you as “wasn’t there”, so know what each one means before you turn this on.

A dropped set, delete, pop or version-bump incr serves stale data. The old entry stays. It’s served until it expires, and with no expiry that means forever, or until a later write replaces it. delete returns False, the same as for a key that wasn’t there, so your code can’t tell. The log line is the only signal. If stale data would be a real problem, give those entries an expiry.
A pop whose delete fails returns the default, not the value, since the row is still there and a later pop could deliver the value a second time.
A fake incr isn’t a count. It’s what a NullCache returns, so a rate limiter fails open. Don’t use one as an id: two callers can get the same number.
add fails closed. It returns False under durable=True, but True on a NullCache, so Caches can give you either answer for one key. Use a separate handle without durable for claims and locks, and treat its exceptions as “not claimed”.

title: Getting started
text:
It doesn’t bound time
A call still waits up to its timeout before it gives up, so pair durable=True with a small timeout=. Not too small: timeout still has to exceed the work in flight, plus a fork, plus the interpreter handing over, or ordinary forks turn into misses. Beside busy threads on a GIL build, that hand-over alone takes tens to hundreds of milliseconds. See How long a call waits for a fork.

title: Getting started
text:
Reporting
Every swallowed failure is counted in one of three groups, and logged on the diskcache_oxide logger, so one group can’t hide another:








Group
Level
What’s in it




Busy
WARNING
Timeout: a lock or a fork outlasted timeout


Failing
ERROR
Everything else: a full disk, an I/O error, a damaged database


Lost invalidations
ERROR
Any failed delete



Each group logs its first failure at once, then at most once a minute per cache handle, with counts by operation since its last line: get: 1204, set: 37. An outage can be thousands of failures a second, and that’s one line a minute. Failures after a group’s last line stay counted until its next one, or until you call close(), which logs what’s left. Dropping a handle without close() doesn’t. An outage that ends within the minute can therefore show only its first failure until then, which is why each line says more may follow. A hook outage on a read is reported once per stored version, as in the pop table above, and counted here as busy for a timeout and failing otherwise, with no line of its own: the group’s next line includes it. Time comes from the failing call’s clock, so clock= drives it in tests. cache._durable_stats() has the running totals by group and operation, the place to look for “how many invalidations did we lose?”. It’s a private hook for now, like _wal_stats().
The limit is per handle, so a with Cache(...) per request logs on every request during an outage. A handle from Caches is opened once, so it isn’t affected.

title: NullCache
text:
Sooner or later you need to turn caching off. In tests, so each one starts clean. In local development, so you see your change instead of yesterday’s. In production, at the worst possible moment, while you chase a bug that might be a stale entry and might not. Without help, that means if cache is not None: around every call, or a hand-written fake that drifts a little further from the real API with every release.
NullCache is a cache that’s switched off. It has the same methods and signatures as Cache, so swapping one for the other is a one-line change, and the code that uses it never knows.

title: NullCache
text:
Watch add()
The rule means add() always succeeds on a NullCache. If you use add() to claim a job so only one worker runs it, then with caching off every worker’s claim succeeds and the job runs once per worker. That’s harmless for idempotent work and wrong for work with side effects, like sending email. Keep claims like that on a cache that’s never switched off.
Cache(durable=True) goes the other way: its add() returns False when a write fails, so a claim fails closed there and open here. Keep claims on a handle that isn’t durable and handle its exceptions. See A cache that can’t take a request down.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
diskcache-oxide’s test suite is a conformance suite: the same black-box tests run against real diskcache 5.6.3 and against diskcache-oxide. Where they behave differently, it’s on purpose, and it’s written down here. Running one suite against two implementations turned out to be a bug detector pointed in both directions: most of the differences below are diskcache bugs the suite found, each with a reproduction in the repository’s upstream/ folder.
A divergence is never a way to skip a failing test. The full record, including test names and measurements, is tests/DIVERGENCES.md.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
D-001: no pickle by default
diskcache pickles every value. diskcache-oxide stores str and bytes raw and everything else as msgpack or tagged JSON. A value the format can’t represent exactly raises TypeError at set() unless the cache was opened with pickle=True. A cache opened without it never unpickles: reading a pickled value written by a pickle=True peer raises UnsafeValueError and leaves the row alone. Unpickling runs code from whatever is in the cache directory, and silently pickling hides values that were never meant to be cached. See Serialization.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
D-015: owner-only directories
A cache directory diskcache-oxide creates, and its value-file subdirectories, are 0700. Existing directories are never changed. Anyone who can write to a cache directory can poison the cache, and its contents (keys with IP addresses in them, for example) can be private.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
D-021: directory is required
diskcache creates a temporary directory if you don’t give one. A cache directory is shared state and a security boundary, and an implicit temp directory is almost never what a multi-process app wants.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
D-008: NaN round-trips
In diskcache, set('k', float('nan')) succeeds but get('k') returns None, ignoring any default. In diskcache-oxide it’s a float like any other.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
section: D-010: expire() removes everything that has expired
text:
D-010: expire() removes everything that has expired
diskcache’s expire() works in chunks of 100, and when expired entries share one expiry time it stops after the first chunk. With 250 such entries, one call removes 100. diskcache-oxide removes all of them, still in chunks so writers can get in between.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
D-011: clear() keeps concurrent writes
diskcache’s clear() keeps deleting until the cache is empty, including entries written while it runs. In a reproduction with 50,000 entries and a concurrent writer, it deleted 76,000 writes that had already succeeded, and its running time grew with the write rate. diskcache-oxide’s clear() removes only entries that existed when it started, and always finishes.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
section: D-013 and D-016: large values under pressure
text:
D-013 and D-016: large values under pressure
If a large value’s file disappears, diskcache returns the default but the key still reads as present in in and len. diskcache-oxide treats it as a miss and removes the orphaned row.
When one process overwrites a large value while others read it, diskcache occasionally returns the default for a key that was never deleted, which makes callers recompute a hot value for nothing. diskcache-oxide’s readers detect the overwrite and retry, so they always get a whole value, old or new.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
D-014: no booleans for numbers
bool is an int subclass, so in diskcache expire=True is a one-second TTL and expire=False stores an already-expired entry. diskcache-oxide raises TypeError: a bool there is almost always an argument in the wrong position.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
section: D-012: forks while another thread writes
text:
D-012: forks while another thread writes
When a process forks while another of its threads is in a write transaction, diskcache’s child inherits a lock nobody in the child will release, and its first write stalls for the full timeout (60 seconds by default). Under a busy read/write load that hits 20-50% of forks. diskcache-oxide’s fork barrier waits for in-flight transactions before the fork, so the child can always write. See Concurrency and forks.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
section: D-020: forking inside your own transaction
text:
D-020: forking inside your own transaction
CPython won’t let a library stop a fork, and a transaction held by the forking thread itself can’t be waited for. In diskcache the child stalls behind it. In diskcache-oxide, the child’s copy of the transaction is poisoned and its writes to that database raise RuntimeError immediately, and the parent gets a RuntimeWarning.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
section: D-029: tx is the cache, and every handle shares it
text:
D-029: tx is the cache, and every handle shares it
diskcache’s with cache.transact() as tx: binds tx to None, and a second Cache on the same directory has its own connection, so its transact() inside the first one’s block waits for the write lock until it times out. In diskcache-oxide tx is the cache itself, and on the thread that entered the block every call on that directory runs in the transaction, through any handle: a transact() on a second handle joins the outer one instead of waiting. Other threads’ calls never join it. See Transactions.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
section: D-030: TransactionBusy, and what retry=True retries
text:
D-030: TransactionBusy, and what retry=True retries
Inside one cache’s transaction, diskcache’s transact() on a second cache waits for its write lock until it times out, and retry=True loops on any sqlite3.OperationalError. When another thread holds that lock, diskcache-oxide raises TransactionBusy, a Timeout subclass, at once: that thread could be waiting for a lock this one holds, and no timeout setting fixes that. retry=True retries a plain Timeout and never TransactionBusy, and checks for Ctrl-C between attempts.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
section: D-031: a transaction can end on another thread
text:
D-031: a transaction can end on another thread
diskcache says a transaction “may not be shared between threads”. In diskcache-oxide any thread may commit or roll back the owner’s transaction through its __exit__, within the transaction’s timeout. A commit that can’t run in time raises Timeout and rolls back, and the owner’s own exit afterwards raises TransactionAborted (a RuntimeError) unless the transaction committed, so a with block never exits cleanly when its writes are gone. An owner’s exit during another thread’s commit waits for the outcome.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
D-017 and D-018: bounded connections
diskcache opens a connection for every thread that uses a cache, so 64 threads hold 131 files open in the cache directory, and close() closes only the calling thread’s connection. diskcache-oxide uses a pool per database file, at most max_connections (default 8), and the last close() closes every connection, so the directory is safe to move or delete afterwards.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
D-019: opening never writes
Opening an existing diskcache commits a write transaction even when nothing changed. diskcache-oxide’s open, and reads after it, never write, so a read-mostly worker or a read-only copy of the directory never takes the write lock.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
D-023: bounded SQLite memory
diskcache’s default is a 32 MiB page cache and a 64 MiB memory map per connection, with one connection per thread. diskcache-oxide’s sqlite_cache_size defaults to 256 pages (1 MiB) per pooled connection, so SQLite’s memory per directory stays around 8 MiB per process.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
D-024: a WAL that shrinks
With readers in other processes, a burst of writes makes SQLite’s write-ahead log grow to fit the burst and stay that size: hundreds of MiB to over 1 GiB beside a database of a few MiB. diskcache-oxide trims the log whenever it resets (wal_size_limit), offers checkpoint() to empty it on demand, checkpoints a large log at close(), and can checkpoint automatically with wal_checkpoint='auto', which tries a few times in a row so that a reader in flight in another process doesn’t defeat it. See Storage and WAL.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
FanoutCache (D-032 to D-040)
These are covered together in FanoutCache: sharded caches, and listed against diskcache’s in Switching from python-diskcache.

D-032: the shard count is part of where every key lives, so it’s recorded, and a different shards= is an error instead of a quiet loss of data and atomicity.
D-033: the hash is fixed by its definition and part of the format, and iterkeys(prefix=) gives FanoutCache the ordered listing Cache has.
D-034: a silently dropped write and a hang are both worse than an error the caller chose how to handle; durable=True is that choice.
D-035: a maintenance job must finish in bounded time, and when it can’t, it must say what it did.
D-036 and D-037: budgets (size, connections, file descriptors) follow configuration, not the number of threads or shards.
D-038: a typo shouldn’t leave a directory that neither kind of cache can open, or a shard written behind the FanoutCache’s back.
D-039: the missing stock features each need their own design across shards, so they arrive with those features on the roadmap rather than as copies.
D-040: holding every shard’s lock would serialize the whole cache behind one transaction, which is what sharding exists to avoid.

title: Running a job once across workers
text:
At the top of the hour, eight gunicorn workers wake up at the same instant with the same idea: time for the hourly cleanup. Each one has its own copy of the scheduler, none of them knows the others exist, and the only thing they share is a cache directory. You want the job to run once, and it turns out the directory is enough.
add() stores a value only if the key is missing or expired, and it’s atomic across every thread and process using the cache directory. When several callers race to add the same key, exactly one gets True. That makes the key a claim on the job.

Claim the run
import os

from diskcache_oxide import Cache

cache = Cache('/var/cache/my-app')

def hourly_cleanup() -> None:
    if not cache.add('job:hourly-cleanup', os.getpid(), expire=55 * 60):
        return  # another worker has it this hour
    remove_stale_sessions()
The expire is the important part. It decides when the job can be claimed again, and it’s also what saves you if the worker that claimed the job crashes halfway through: the claim expires and the next run goes ahead. Set it a little shorter than the schedule’s interval, so the next run is never blocked by the previous claim.
Storing os.getpid() (or a hostname and pid) as the value costs nothing and makes it easy to see who claimed the job: cache.get('job:hourly-cleanup').


See it work
Here eight threads race for the same claim. Processes behave the same way.

import tempfile
import threading

from diskcache_oxide import Cache

cache = Cache(tempfile.mkdtemp())
winners = []
start = threading.Barrier(8)

def worker(n: int) -> None:
    start.wait()
    if cache.add('job:hourly-cleanup', n, expire=3300):
        winners.append(n)

threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(n,)) for n in range(8)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()

print(f'{len(winners)} winner: worker {winners[0]}')
print('claim holds:', cache.get('job:hourly-cleanup'))

1 winner: worker 7
claim holds: 7




Jobs that should run once, then again as soon as they’re done
For work that isn’t on a fixed schedule (process the queue, rebuild the search index), use expire as a lease: a time limit after which a crashed worker’s claim lapses. Delete the key when the work finishes, so the next request can claim it right away.
def rebuild_search_index() -> None:
    if not cache.add('job:search-index', os.getpid(), expire=10 * 60):
        return
    try:
        do_rebuild()
    finally:
        cache.delete('job:search-index')
Make the lease comfortably longer than the job ever takes. If the job outlives it, a second worker can start a second copy.


Give claims their own small cache
Two things can make a claim vanish early, and both argue for keeping claims out of your main cache:

Switching caching off. A NullCache follows the rule “every entry expires the instant it’s written”, so its add() always returns True. With caching off, every worker’s claim succeeds and the job runs once per worker. That’s harmless for idempotent jobs and wrong for jobs with side effects, like sending email.
Eviction. When a cache is over its size_limit, it evicts the least recently stored entries, and a claim is exactly the kind of small, rarely written entry that goes first. If it’s evicted before it expires, a second worker can claim the job.

A separate cache directory just for coordination, which is never swapped for a NullCache and holds only a handful of tiny keys, avoids both:
coordination = Cache('/var/cache/my-app-coordination')
Proper cross-process Lock and BoundedSemaphore recipes are planned (see the roadmap).
crumbs: Running a job once across workers

title: Counting things
text:
A download counter is the simplest feature on the site, and the first one to start lying once there’s more than one worker: each process counts what it saw, and the number on the page depends on which worker rendered it. Moving the count to the database fixes the lie and makes every download a write to your busiest table. A cache counter sits in between: incr() is atomic across every thread and process on the machine, costs tens of microseconds, and the totals can be moved to the database on a schedule, by one worker, without losing a single count on the way.

Count from every worker

import tempfile
import threading

from diskcache_oxide import Cache

cache = Cache(tempfile.mkdtemp())

def record_view(episode_id: int) -> None:
    cache.incr(f'views:episode:{episode_id}')

def viewer() -> None:
    for _ in range(250):
        record_view(512)

threads = [threading.Thread(target=viewer) for _ in range(8)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()

print(cache.get('views:episode:512'), 'views, none lost')

2000 views, none lost


incr() starts a missing counter at default (0) and adds delta (1), so there’s no setup step. Processes behave exactly like the threads here.


Flush the counts to the database
Totals belong in the database eventually: for reports, and so they survive a cleared cache. pop() reads a counter and removes it in one atomic step, so a view recorded while the flush runs lands in a fresh counter and is picked up next time. Nothing is counted twice or lost.

database: dict[int, int] = {}   # stands in for UPDATE episodes SET views = views + ? WHERE id = ?

def flush_views() -> None:
    for key in cache.iterkeys(prefix='views:episode:'):
        pending = cache.pop(key, 0)
        if pending:
            episode_id = int(key.rsplit(':', 1)[1])
            database[episode_id] = database.get(episode_id, 0) + pending

record_view(513)
flush_views()
print('database:', database, '| pending in cache:', cache.get('views:episode:512', 0))

database: {512: 2000, 513: 1} | pending in cache: 0


Run the flush from one place, a scheduled job that one worker claims, every minute or so. To show a live total, add the pending count to the stored one: database[id] + cache.get(key, 0).


Counters that clean themselves up
For per-day or per-month figures, put the period in the key and give each counter an expiry. Create it with add() first: incr() keeps whatever expiry the key already has, and on a key it has to create, it sets none.

import datetime

def record_download(file_id: str, day: datetime.date) -> int:
    key = f'downloads:{file_id}:{day.isoformat()}'
    cache.add(key, 0, expire=40 * 24 * 3600)   # keep 40 days of history
    return cache.incr(key)

today = datetime.date(2026, 11, 8)
record_download('talk-python-491.mp3', today)
print(record_download('talk-python-491.mp3', today), 'downloads today')

2 downloads today


To report a week, read the seven keys. Old days expire on their own, so the cache never fills with history.


Quotas with decr()
A quota is a counter that starts at the allowance and counts down:

def consume_quota(user_id: int, units: int = 1, allowance: int = 1000) -> bool:
    key = f'quota:{user_id}:2026-11'                       # the billing period, in a real app from the date
    cache.add(key, allowance, expire=40 * 24 * 3600)      # the first call this period sets the allowance
    return cache.decr(key, units) >= 0

print(consume_quota(42, units=999), consume_quota(42), consume_quota(42))

True True False


Once the counter is below zero every later call is denied too, until the period’s key is replaced. To let an admin grant more, incr() the key by the extra amount. delta can be a float, for fractional units.


Several counters at once
Counting a request under several keys (total, per path, per status) is three incr() calls, and a reader can see the first land before the third. If that matters, put them in one transaction: the block commits all of them together.


Things to know

A missing counter reads as default. When a missing counter is a bug rather than a zero, pass default=None and incr() raises KeyError instead.
Counters need a real cache. A NullCache has nothing to count in: its incr() returns default + delta every time, so every view would be the first. Keep counters in a cache that’s never switched off, which Caches lets you do per name.
durable=True drops counts silently. A failed incr() returns default + delta so a rate limiter fails open, but for a quota or a view count that’s a lost increment with only a log line to show for it. Let these raise, and catch Timeout where you call them.
Not an id generator. Two callers can get the same number back under durable=True, and a cleared cache restarts at zero. Ids come from the database.
One machine. Every worker on a host shares the counts; two hosts behind a load balancer each have their own, so flush each host’s counts to the database and sum there.

title: Storing your own types
text:
The first TypeError from set() is a small shock. You’ve been storing dicts for weeks, and today one of them has a UUID in it and the cache says no. That refusal is the design: the cache stores the built-in types exactly (Serialization has the table: str, numbers, bytes, bool, None, lists, tuples, sets, dicts, datetime, date, Decimal) and refuses anything else rather than pickling it behind your back. For everything else, you tell the codec once how to store the type, and the shock never comes back. This recipe collects the registrations a typical web app needs.

The standard library’s types
uuid.UUID, datetime.timedelta and pathlib.Path aren’t built-in types to the codec. Each needs an encode that turns an instance into something storable and a decode that turns it back:

import datetime
import pathlib
import tempfile
import uuid

import diskcache_oxide
from diskcache_oxide import Cache

diskcache_oxide.register_type(uuid.UUID, name='std.uuid', encode=lambda u: u.bytes, decode=lambda b: uuid.UUID(bytes=b))
diskcache_oxide.register_type(datetime.timedelta, name='std.timedelta', encode=datetime.timedelta.total_seconds, decode=lambda s: datetime.timedelta(seconds=s))
diskcache_oxide.register_type(type(pathlib.Path()), name='std.path', encode=str, decode=pathlib.Path)

cache = Cache(tempfile.mkdtemp())
cache.set('upload', {'id': uuid.uuid4(), 'ttl': datetime.timedelta(hours=2), 'file': pathlib.Path('/srv/uploads/a.png')})
print({k: type(v).__name__ for k, v in cache.get('upload').items()})

{'id': 'UUID', 'ttl': 'timedelta', 'file': 'PosixPath'}


The Path registration says type(pathlib.Path()), not pathlib.Path, for a reason: lookup is by exact type, and pathlib.Path() builds a PosixPath or a WindowsPath. Registering the base class would match nothing. The same applies to any factory that returns a subclass.


Enums
Store the value, and let the enum class turn it back into a member. A StrEnum or IntEnum is a subclass of str or int, and a subclass is never stored as its base, so it needs this too:

import enum

class Plan(enum.StrEnum):
    FREE = 'free'
    PRO = 'pro'

diskcache_oxide.register_type(Plan, name='app.Plan', encode=lambda p: p.value, decode=Plan)

cache.set('account:42:plan', Plan.PRO)
print(repr(cache.get('account:42:plan')))

<Plan.PRO: 'pro'>




Dataclasses
A dataclass needs only a name. Its fields are stored and it’s rebuilt with cls(**fields), so defaults and __post_init__ run. Fields can hold other registered types, nested as deep as you like:

import dataclasses

@dataclasses.dataclass
class Invoice:
    id: uuid.UUID
    plan: Plan
    issued: datetime.date
    paid_within: datetime.timedelta | None = None

diskcache_oxide.register_type(Invoice, name='app.Invoice')

cache.set('invoice:latest', Invoice(uuid.UUID('2b7e1c4a-5d3f-4e8b-9a6c-0f1d2e3a4b5c'), Plan.PRO, datetime.date(2026, 11, 8)))
print(cache.get('invoice:latest'))

Invoice(id=UUID('2b7e1c4a-5d3f-4e8b-9a6c-0f1d2e3a4b5c'), plan=<Plan.PRO: 'pro'>, issued=datetime.date(2026, 11, 8), paid_within=None)




Pydantic models
Pydantic can produce and consume a plain dict, so a model registers with its own two methods. mode='json' makes model_dump() emit only JSON-compatible values (UUIDs and dates as strings), which model_validate() parses back, so the model’s field types need no registrations of their own:
from pydantic import BaseModel

class User(BaseModel):
    id: uuid.UUID
    name: str
    plan: Plan

diskcache_oxide.register_type(User, name='app.User', encode=lambda u: u.model_dump(mode='json'), decode=User.model_validate)
attrs classes and msgspec structs follow the same pattern with attrs.asdict() and msgspec.to_builtins(), and the class as the decoder.


Where the registrations live
Registrations are process-wide and must exist in every process that opens the directory: the web workers, the Celery workers, the management command that warms the cache. A row written with a tag the reading process doesn’t know is a ForeignValueError, and the row is left for a process that does. Put them in one module and import it early:
# myapp/cache_types.py: imported from myapp/__init__.py, so every entry point gets it
import diskcache_oxide

from myapp.models import Invoice, Plan, User

diskcache_oxide.register_type(Plan, name='app.Plan', encode=lambda p: p.value, decode=Plan)
diskcache_oxide.register_type(Invoice, name='app.Invoice')
diskcache_oxide.register_type(User, name='app.User', encode=lambda u: u.model_dump(mode='json'), decode=User.model_validate)


When the shape changes
The name is the contract. Renaming or moving the class changes nothing, because rows carry the name you chose. Changing the fields does: a dataclass row written before a required field was added raises CorruptValueError when it’s read, and on_decode_error='miss' turns that into a miss and deletes the row, so the next writer replaces it. For a change the old rows can’t survive, give the type a new name (app.Invoice.v2). The old rows become ForeignValueError, treated as misses under the same policy, and expire on their own. See Errors.

title: Recipes
text:
A shared cache does more jobs in a real app than caching. It elects a worker, counts requests, holds sessions and one-time tokens, remembers what was invalidated, and stands in for Redis wherever Redis was only ever there to hold a counter. Each recipe below starts with the moment you’d reach for one, then shows the pattern, then says where it stops working. The examples with output under them execute against diskcache-oxide every time these docs are built, so they’re known to work, not merely believed to.

Caching
Caching expensive calls. The cache-aside pattern, and a small decorator that turns any function into a cached one, with keys built safely from its arguments.
Serving stale values while refreshing. Keep a slow page or report available while one worker rebuilds it in the background, or refresh the hot keys ahead of time from a job, so readers never wait and the thundering herd is one worker.
Caching responses from other services. Cache an upstream API’s answers, honor its max-age, revalidate with ETags, and keep serving the last good answer when it’s down.
Invalidating groups of keys. Clear everything cached for one user, one product or one page at once: delete by key prefix, or bump a generation number so stale entries are never read again.
Storing your own types. UUIDs, enums, timedeltas, Paths, dataclasses and Pydantic models in the cache with one registration each, and no pickle.


Coordinating workers
Running a job once across workers. Eight gunicorn workers each schedule the same hourly job, and you want it to run once. add() is atomic across processes, so exactly one of them claims it.
Rate limiting. Count requests per client in fixed time windows with add() and incr(), shared by every worker on the machine, with no Redis.
Counting things. View counts, download totals and usage quotas with incr() and decr(), flushed to the database with pop() so no count is lost or doubled.
Single-use keys. Reset links, verification codes and idempotency keys: pop() hands a value to exactly one caller, and add() accepts a key exactly once.


State
Server-side sessions. Sessions every worker can read, with a sliding idle timeout from touch(), an absolute lifetime, and log-out-everywhere by key prefix.


Deployment and testing
Sharing a cache across web workers. Where to put the cache directory, when to open it with gunicorn, uvicorn, FastAPI, Flask, Django and Celery, how to keep a busy cache from slowing requests, and what to do at shutdown.
Using the cache from asyncio. Read inline, write off the loop, and keep transactions on one thread, in FastAPI, Starlette or aiohttp, until AsyncCache lands.
Testing code that uses a cache. pytest fixtures for a real cache in a temporary directory, a NullCache for tests that shouldn’t cache at all, and a fake clock for testing expiry without sleeping.


Coming later
More recipes will arrive with the features they need: memoize with stampede protection, tags, cross-process locks and throttles, and AsyncCache for asyncio apps. FanoutCache and transact() are here already and have their own guide pages. See the roadmap.

title: Caching expensive calls
text:
The page takes 900 ms, and 850 of them are one query that returns the same ten rows it returned a second ago. Everyone has met this page. Caching is how you stop paying for the same answer twice: before doing something slow (a database query, an API call, rendering a big page), ask the cache. If it knows, you’re done in a microsecond or two. If not, do the work and leave the answer for whoever asks next, which with a shared directory means every worker process on the machine, today and after the next restart.

Cache-aside

import tempfile
import time

from diskcache_oxide import Cache

cache = Cache(tempfile.mkdtemp())

def load_popular_episodes() -> list[dict]:
    time.sleep(0.2)  # stands in for a slow database query
    return [{'id': 512, 'title': 'Rust for Python developers'}]

def popular_episodes() -> list[dict]:
    episodes = cache.get('episodes:popular')
    if episodes is None:
        episodes = load_popular_episodes()
        cache.set('episodes:popular', episodes, expire=300)
    return episodes

start = time.perf_counter()
popular_episodes()
print(f'first call:  {(time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000:.1f} ms')

start = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(1000):
    popular_episodes()
print(f'cached:      {(time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000:.1f} µs per call')  # 1000 calls, so ms total = µs each

first call:  202.7 ms
cached:      1.1 µs per call


Always give cached values an expire. It bounds how stale a value can get if an invalidation is ever missed.


When None is a real value
If the function can legitimately return None, cache.get(key) can’t tell “cached as None” from “not cached”, and you’ll recompute every time. Use a sentinel default:
MISSING = object()

value = cache.get(key, default=MISSING)
if value is MISSING:
    value = compute()
    cache.set(key, value, expire=300)


A caching decorator
The same pattern wrapped up for reuse. The key is the function’s full name plus its arguments, encoded as JSON so that different arguments always give different keys.

import functools
import json
from collections.abc import Callable
from typing import Any

from diskcache_oxide import CacheLike

MISSING = object()

def cached(cache: CacheLike, expire: float | None = None) -> Callable:
    """Cache a function's results, keyed by its arguments."""

    def decorator(func: Callable) -> Callable:
        prefix = f'{func.__module__}.{func.__qualname__}:'

        @functools.wraps(func)
        def wrapper(*args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> Any:
            key = prefix + json.dumps([args, kwargs], sort_keys=True, default=str)
            value = cache.get(key, default=MISSING)
            if value is MISSING:
                value = func(*args, **kwargs)
                cache.set(key, value, expire=expire)
            return value

        return wrapper

    return decorator

calls = 0

@cached(cache, expire=600)
def episode_details(episode_id: int, *, include_transcript: bool = False) -> dict:
    global calls
    calls += 1
    return {'id': episode_id, 'transcript': include_transcript}

episode_details(512)
episode_details(512)
episode_details(512, include_transcript=True)
print(f'{calls} real calls for 3 lookups')

2 real calls for 3 lookups


A few things to keep in mind:

Arguments become part of the key, so keep them simple: ids, strings, numbers. default=str covers values like dates, but two different objects with the same str() would share a key.
Return values must be storable, which means built-in types (dicts, lists, tuples, sets, datetimes and so on). A dataclass or ORM object raises TypeError at set(): return a dict instead, or use a cache opened with pickle=True. See Serialization.
Long keys are fine. A key is just an indexed string.



Thundering herds
When a popular entry expires, every worker that asks for it in the next moment misses at the same time, and all of them recompute it. For most values that’s harmless. If the computation is expensive enough that doing it eight times at once hurts, refresh it ahead of expiry from a background job (see Running a job once across workers), so readers never see it missing.
A memoize with built-in stampede protection is planned (see the roadmap).

title: Invalidating groups of keys
text:
A user changes their display name, and for the next five minutes half the site still uses the old one: the profile page, the sidebar widget, three API responses, each cached on its own schedule and each wrong in its own way. A single change often makes many cache entries stale, and deleting them one by one means knowing every key that was ever derived from that user. There are two good ways to handle this. Both start with a naming convention.

Name keys hierarchically
Put the thing a key depends on at the front of the key, from the general to the specific:
user:42:profile
user:42:sidebar
user:42:api:/v1/me
episode:512:page
episode:512:transcript
Everything about user 42 now shares the prefix user:42:. Note the trailing colon: without it, user:4 would also match user:42.


Option 1: delete by prefix
iterkeys(prefix=...) is an indexed range scan, so finding a user’s keys costs time in proportion to how many there are, not the size of the cache. It fetches keys a page at a time with no lock held in between, so deleting while iterating is safe.

import tempfile

from diskcache_oxide import Cache

cache = Cache(tempfile.mkdtemp())
for key in ['user:42:profile', 'user:42:sidebar', 'user:420:profile', 'episode:512:page']:
    cache.set(key, '...', expire=3600)

def invalidate_prefix(prefix: str) -> int:
    removed = 0
    for key in cache.iterkeys(prefix=prefix):
        removed += cache.delete(key)
    return removed

print(invalidate_prefix('user:42:'), 'removed')
print(sorted(cache))

2 removed
['episode:512:page', 'user:420:profile']


This is simple and frees the space right away. It costs one small write per key, so it’s best when a group has tens or hundreds of keys, not hundreds of thousands.


Option 2: generation numbers
Instead of deleting anything, keep a generation number per group and put it in every key. To invalidate the group, change the generation. Every old key becomes unreachable at once, in a single write, however many keys there were. The old entries are never read again, and they leave the cache when they expire or are evicted.

import time

def generation(user_id: int) -> int:
    key = f'gen:user:{user_id}'
    gen = cache.get(key)
    if gen is None:
        cache.add(key, time.time_ns())   # if several workers race, one value wins
        gen = cache.get(key)
    return gen

def user_key(user_id: int, name: str) -> str:
    return f'user:{user_id}:g{generation(user_id)}:{name}'

def invalidate_user(user_id: int) -> None:
    cache.set(f'gen:user:{user_id}', time.time_ns())

cache.set(user_key(7, 'profile'), {'name': 'Sam'}, expire=3600)
print(cache.get(user_key(7, 'profile')))

invalidate_user(7)
print(cache.get(user_key(7, 'profile')))

{'name': 'Sam'}
None


Generation numbers cost one extra read per lookup (the generation, which is tiny and hot) and make invalidation free. Give the real entries an expire, since nothing deletes them.
The generations are timestamps rather than a counter starting at 0 for a reason. A generation key is written rarely, and the cache evicts the least recently stored entries first, so under size pressure it can be evicted. A counter would then restart at 0 and bring old entries back to life. A new timestamp is always larger than any generation used before, so a lost generation only costs a few cache misses.


Which to use

Prefix deletes when groups are small and you want the space back immediately.
Generation numbers when groups are large, or invalidation is frequent, or many workers might invalidate the same group at the same time.



While caching is switched off
If you turn caching off with NullCache, pass the real cache as invalidate=. Prefix deletes still reach the real cache (iterkeys and delete are both forwarded), so nothing stale is waiting when caching comes back on. See NullCache.
Tags, which group keys without a naming convention, are planned (see the roadmap).

title: Serving stale values while refreshing
text:
The newsletter goes out at 9:00. At 9:00:01, four hundred readers land on the front page, and the cached copy expired at 8:59:58. Every worker misses at the same instant, every one of them starts rendering the same page, and the database spends its morning answering one question four hundred times. The caching recipe calls this a thundering herd. For most values it’s harmless. When the value is slow to build (a front page that takes 400 ms, a report that queries a warehouse), there are two ways to make sure readers never see the gap, and only one worker does the work.

Stale-while-revalidate
Store the value with its own freshness deadline inside, and give the entry a longer hard expiry. A reader that finds the entry fresh returns it. One that finds it stale returns it anyway, and the first of them to win a claim starts a refresh in the background. Readers never wait, and the herd is one worker.

import tempfile
import threading
import time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from typing import Any

from diskcache_oxide import Cache

now = [1_000_000.0]                                   # a fake clock; in a real app use time.time()
cache = Cache(tempfile.mkdtemp(), clock=lambda: now[0])
refresher = ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2)         # one per process, for background refreshes
loads: list[float] = []

def load_front_page() -> dict:
    time.sleep(0.05)                                  # stands in for 400 ms of rendering
    loads.append(now[0])
    return {'rendered_at': now[0]}

def store(key: str, value: Any, fresh_for: float, grace: float) -> Any:
    cache.set(key, {'value': value, 'fresh_until': now[0] + fresh_for}, expire=fresh_for + grace)
    return value

def refresh(key: str, fresh_for: float, grace: float) -> None:
    try:
        store(key, load_front_page(), fresh_for, grace)
    finally:
        cache.delete(f'refresh:{key}')

def front_page(fresh_for: float = 60, grace: float = 300) -> dict:
    key = 'page:front'
    entry = cache.get(key)
    if entry is None:                                 # a real miss: nothing to serve, compute inline
        return store(key, load_front_page(), fresh_for, grace)
    if now[0] >= entry['fresh_until'] and cache.add(f'refresh:{key}', 1, expire=30):
        refresher.submit(refresh, key, fresh_for, grace)   # stale, and this worker won the refresh
    return entry['value']                             # fresh or stale, the reader gets it now

front_page()                                          # the first request renders the page
now[0] += 61                                          # a minute later it's stale

results = []
start = threading.Barrier(8)

def request() -> None:
    start.wait()
    results.append(front_page()['rendered_at'])

threads = [threading.Thread(target=request) for _ in range(8)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()
refresher.shutdown(wait=True)                         # in the example only: let the refresh land

print(f'{len(results)} readers got the stale page from t={results[0]:.0f}, {len(loads)} renders in total')
print(f"the next reader gets the fresh page from t={front_page()['rendered_at']:.0f}")

8 readers got the stale page from t=1000000, 2 renders in total
the next reader gets the fresh page from t=1000061


The three numbers to choose:

fresh_for is how old a value may get before a refresh starts. It plays the role expire plays in a plain cache.
grace is how much longer the stale value stays available. If no refresh lands within it (the refresher crashed, the source was down), the entry expires and the next reader computes inline, herd and all. Make it generous: minutes, not seconds.
The claim’s expire (30 s here) bounds how long a crashed refresher blocks the next one. Make it longer than a refresh ever takes.

In an asyncio app, start the refresh with asyncio.create_task(asyncio.to_thread(refresh, ...)) instead of a thread pool; see Using the cache from asyncio. With durable=True, a failed add() returns False, so nobody refreshes until the cache is healthy again, which is the right outcome.


Refreshing ahead from a job
When the hot keys are known in advance (the front page, the top ten episodes, the pricing table), it’s simpler to never let them go stale: a scheduled job, claimed by one worker, recomputes them every few minutes and stores each with an expire of at least twice the interval.
HOT_PAGES = ['front', 'episodes', 'pricing']

def refresh_hot_pages() -> None:                      # runs every 5 minutes, on one worker
    if not coordination.add('job:refresh-hot-pages', os.getpid(), expire=4 * 60):
        return
    for name in HOT_PAGES:
        cache.set(f'page:{name}', render_page(name), expire=15 * 60)
Readers do a plain get() and never miss; a missed run or two costs nothing because the entries outlive several intervals. The cost is that the job renders pages nobody may be asking for, which is fine for a handful of keys and wrong for a long tail. Stale-while-revalidate handles the tail, since it only refreshes what’s being read.
A memoize decorator with this built in is planned (see the roadmap).

This changelog is generated automatically from GitHub Releases.

v0.1.0
2026-11-09 · GitHub
The first release: diskcache’s Cache API on a Rust engine and SQLite storage, shared safely by threads, processes and fork(), on CPython 3.14 and 3.15 including the free-threaded builds. Wheels for macOS on Apple Silicon and Linux (glibc) on x86_64 and aarch64.

Added

Cache, API compatible with diskcache 5.6.3’s Cache: get, set, add, incr/decr, pop, delete, touch, expire, cull, clear, iterkeys, len, volume, size limits with least-recently-stored eviction, and the mapping methods. It passes a conformance suite run against diskcache itself, apart from the documented divergences.
FanoutCache, which shards keys over several databases so many writing processes don’t queue on one write lock.
transact() on both, which lands several writes together or none of them, with TransactionBusy and TransactionAborted.
Values stored as msgpack (the default) or JSON, with exact type tags for tuples, sets, datetimes, big ints and NaN. A value that can’t round-trip exactly raises TypeError at set(). register_type() stores your own types and a library’s without pickle, a dataclass with only a name; pickle=True is opt-in per cache, and a cache without it never unpickles.
durable=True, which answers an outage (a busy lock, a full disk) as a miss and logs it at most once a minute, and on_decode_error= for values that can’t be read.
NullCache, which turns caching off without changing call sites, and Caches, a registry that names an app’s caches, opens each on first use and hands out a NullCache while one can’t open.
Fork safety: a process-wide fork barrier so no child is born holding half a transaction, and caches that keep working in the child.
Bounded resources: at most max_connections SQLite connections per cache directory, a page cache per connection, a write-ahead log that trims itself back to half of wal_size_limit, and checkpoint().
CacheLike, TransactionalCacheLike and ShardedCacheLike protocols, py.typed, and full docstrings in the stubs.
A bundled SQLite (sqlite_version(), sqlite_compile_options()), so the system’s version doesn’t matter.
Documentation: a user guide, recipes, an errors page, an API reference, an agent skill and llms.txt, at https://mkennedy.codes/docs/diskcache-oxide/.



Differences from diskcache

Not data compatible: data lives in diskcache-oxide.sqlite, and diskcache’s cache.db is never opened or converted, so a switched app starts cold.
Keys are str only, directory is required, size_limit must be at least 1 MiB, new cache directories are owner-only (0700), Timeout is a TimeoutError, and bool(cache) is always True.
clear() keeps writes that land while it runs, expire() removes every expired entry, and a read during an overwrite never misses. Each is a diskcache bug, with a standalone repro in the repository’s upstream/ folder.



Not yet
memoize, tags, AsyncCache, Deque and Index, keys other than str, disk=, other eviction policies, the coordination recipes (locks, semaphores, throttles), and Windows. See the roadmap.
Development before this release, including the 0.1.0.dev builds (0.1.0.dev1 was yanked from PyPI), is in the git history. The 0.0.1 on PyPI is a name placeholder with no code.
